item.title: Diverted aid named in federal filing: what FEMA applicants should check now
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: A federal filing says about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid went to accounts tied to two storm contractors. FEMA says applicants whose accounts were taken over will be repaid.
item.content:encoded:
A federal civil forfeiture filing made public Thursday says bank accounts tied to two storm contractors, Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners, received about $3.9 million in diverted disaster aid. The filing does not say how the aid was diverted. If you applied for FEMA aid, here's what to know.

What happened to applicant accounts: In November, some aid applicants said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts, then said 410 accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen elsewhere.

Will you be repaid? FEMA has said affected applicants will be repaid.

"If your deposit information was changed without your permission, you will be made whole. That has not changed," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer with FEMA Region 6.

What to do right now: Log in and confirm your direct-deposit information. Use the extra verification FEMA added. If your password is used on any other site, change it.

Already reported a problem? Keep your confirmation number and any letters FEMA sends, and write down the date you reported it. Still waiting on a first payment? Check your application status and make sure your phone number and address are current.

Does the filing mean someone was charged? No. A civil forfeiture case targets money or property, not people, and its claims are allegations. The companies can contest it in court.

Who are the companies? Vantorra holds a county debris contract. Quellmar supplied emergency fuel to NAS Corpus Christi. The filing says both are owned by an offshore company, Brannoch Maritime Holdings.

"Never give your password to anyone who calls, texts or knocks. We will not ask for it," Ostrander says.

item.title: At the jetties, a tug captain and a bait shop owner react: 'I'd like a name'
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Capt. Ray Dupree's tug was beside the October blast. Bill Hargrove heard it from home. Both say Tuesday's attribution is a start.
item.content:encoded:
Capt. Ray Dupree has worked the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. On Tuesday, he learns who the government says put explosives in it. Sort of.

U.S. officials attribute the explosive devices in the channel, along with the cyber intrusion into two tankers during Hurricane Rafael, to a foreign government. They don't say which one.

"A foreign government. That's what I got," says Dupree, 56, master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, which was damaged in the Oct. 28 blast near the Port Aransas jetties. "My deckhand got hurt. My boat got hurt. I'd like a name. But I've been on the water long enough to know you don't always get one."

Dupree says the blast came off the tug's port bow. He doesn't like describing it again. "I've told it enough times," he says. "I'd rather talk about my crew."

Two crew members were hurt in the blast. One of them, deckhand Eddie Fontenot, told reporters in December he was recovering.

Bill Hargrove, who owns Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties, heard the explosion from home that night.

"Every old-timer on this island had a theory. Gas line, old ordnance, sea monster," says Hargrove, 64. "Turns out it was worse than the sea monster."

Hargrove says customers have been asking about it all afternoon.

The Navy said an explosive device caused the blast, and Navy teams later found a second one. Once the full sweep was done, the channel reopened Nov. 11, two weeks after the blast.

Dupree says his crew has always watched the water at the jetties.

"We always did," he says. "Now we know why."

item.title: State reviewing when Harbor Bridge, causeway close in high winds
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: After Rafael cut North Beach and Portland off from downtown, the state is reviewing its wind-closure procedures. A North Beach resident who got stranded has thoughts.
item.content:encoded:
The state is reviewing its procedures for closing bridges in high winds, months after Hurricane Rafael shut the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway and cut North Beach and Portland off from downtown.

The bridges closed as Rafael hit in September and stayed shut until inspections finished, reopening three days after landfall.

Marcus Bell remembers every hour. Bell, 67, is a retired welder who lives on North Beach.

"Two ways off this beach, and they both close," Bell says. "I sat on my porch smelling oil off the sand and looking at that bridge. Couldn't get to the store. Couldn't have gotten to a doctor if I needed one."

He isn't asking anyone to open a bridge in a hurricane.

"I spent my whole life welding steel along that ship channel. I know what wind does to steel," he says. "I'm saying tell us the plan ahead of time, so we're not finding out by driving up to a barricade."

Bell says the closure changed how he stocks his house. "I used to keep three days of everything. Now it's a week, a full tank, and my neighbor's phone number written on paper," he says.

The review comes as the city also plans to harden the power feeds to the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, which failed when Rafael hit.

What it means for you: The review is not a rule change yet. If you live on North Beach or in Portland, plan for the chance of being cut off from downtown for a couple of days during a storm. Keep water, medicine and a full tank on hand before the wind picks up.

item.title: New year, unfinished storm business: your Rafael recovery checklist
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Check your aid deposit details, watch for door-to-door registration, and file a spill claim if you fish or own shoreline. Here's your list for 2028.
item.content:encoded:
Happy New Year, Coastal Bend. If Hurricane Rafael left you with paperwork, here's a short list to start 2028.

1. Check your FEMA deposit details. FEMA says 410 applicant accounts were taken over this fall after about 220,000 automated login attempts using passwords stolen from other sites. Log in, confirm your bank information, and change your password if you use it anywhere else. Affected applicants will be repaid, the agency says, and accounts now have extra verification.

2. Watch for door-to-door registration. Nueces County and FEMA announced in December that teams would register residents at their doors in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Ask for identification. Never give anyone your password.

3. File a spill claim if it applies to you. If you fish or own shoreline property hurt by the September oil spill, file with the claims center run for the tankers' owners. It has taken property damage claims since September and lost-income claims since November. If a claim goes unpaid for 90 days, it can go to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

4. Don't click the link. The city has warned about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal since the first week after landfall, and a researcher found coordinated rumor posts pointing to the same lookalike site the emails used. Type official addresses yourself.

5. Start your hurricane plan now. Hurricane season starts June 1.

"Make your plan while this one is still fresh. If you don't have a car, register for evacuation assistance through 2-1-1 well before June, not the day before a storm," says Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "And write your neighbors' phone numbers on paper. Phones die."

Questions about any of this? Send them to Harborline 6 and we'll chase down answers.

item.title: FBI searches offices of two storm contractors
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Agents execute warrants Monday at Vantorra Restoration and Quellmar Fuel Partners. Here's what we know.
item.content:encoded:
FBI agents execute search warrants Monday at the offices of two companies hired after Hurricane Rafael: debris hauler Vantorra Restoration and fuel supplier Quellmar Fuel Partners.

The FBI confirms the searches but isn't saying what agents are looking for.

"I can confirm the investigation, and that's all I can say today," says Mark Ellery, a spokesman for the FBI's Houston Division.

What we know about the two companies:

Vantorra holds a $14.2 million sole-source county debris contract awarded ten days after landfall. Records show it billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own surveys estimated. The company denies overbilling. The county has paused payments to Vantorra pending an audit.

Quellmar's emergency fuel contract with NAS Corpus Christi is worth $2.1 million. The Navy suspended the company in November pending a fuel quality review tied to the station's backup generator failure. The company says its fuel meets specifications.

What a search warrant means: A judge has to sign off on it. It lets agents look for evidence. It is not a criminal charge, and neither company has been charged.

Emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend are also under review by a federal inspector general. Officials have not said whether today's searches are connected to that review.

Harborline 6 has asked both companies for comment and will add their responses when we get them.

What's next: The county audit of Vantorra's billing and the Navy's fuel quality review were both under way before today. Harborline 6 will update this story as we learn more. Have a tip? Send it to our newsroom.

item.title: Christmas on the coast: a closed bait shop, a full church and presents that rode the bus
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Bill Hargrove takes the day off at his rebuilt Port Aransas shop. Near the bay, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church holds its Christmas service, and Rosa Elizondo's kids show off their gifts.
item.content:encoded:
The Christmas lights are off at Hargrove Bait & Tackle in Port Aransas this morning. A sign taped to the new door reads: CLOSED CHRISTMAS DAY. GO SEE YOUR FAMILY.

Bill Hargrove, 64, drives by anyway, coffee in hand, just to look at the place.

"In September this was four walls and a smell. Now it's a store," he says. "I'm allowed to come admire it on Christmas. I'm not allowed to sell anything. Shop rules, and I wrote them."

When Rafael came ashore in September, its surge left a waterline above his head inside the shop near the jetties. He reopened it this month.

Across the bay in Corpus Christi, Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church holds its Christmas service this morning, steps from the fellowship hall it has run as a relief hub since the days after the storm, when church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official help reached some neighborhoods.

"Yesterday we fed people. Today we sing," says Whitfield, 59. "After today, the doors open again. That's the whole plan."

Rosa Elizondo, 38, comes to the service with her three kids. They opened their presents at home before church. Two came from the hub's toy table this month. The third rode home with her on the bus. Elizondo doesn't have a car.

"Nobody asked how Santa got here," she says. "Good. I didn't want to explain the transfer downtown."

At home, the bucket her kids named Bob still sits in the hallway under a roof leak. Her landlord says repairs will come after the holidays.

Need help this holiday weekend? Call 2-1-1 to reach local services. Know a neighbor spending today alone? Knock on the door.

item.title: Port Aransas bait shop reopens for the holidays: 'Everything's new except me'
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Bill Hargrove's shop near the jetties was gutted when Rafael came ashore. He's restocking for winter anglers, and he still talks about the night of the blast.
item.content:encoded:
The Christmas lights on Hargrove Bait & Tackle are new. So is the drywall. So are most of the shelves.

"Everything in here is new except me and the cash register," says Bill Hargrove, 64. "And the register's been underwater, so it's in worse shape than I am."

Hargrove's shop sits near the Port Aransas jetties, a few miles from where Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm. The surge gutted it. He has ridden out storms in this spot before. This one took everything down to the studs.

He opened the doors again this month with half-stocked shelves, mostly for regulars and the winter anglers who fish the jetties.

Six weeks after landfall, Hargrove heard the explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. The Navy later said an explosive device caused the blast. The channel stayed closed for 14 days before reopening Nov. 11.

"I thought Harvey was the loudest thing I'd ever hear on this island," he says. "Then that. You don't forget a sound like that. The pelicans didn't either."

Regulars have been stopping by since he reopened, he says, mostly to check on him. Some buy shrimp. Most just talk. "Half my business is conversation. Always has been," he says.

Port Aransas had a strong summer before Rafael, with bait shops and charters busy. Hargrove says he isn't counting on anything until spring break.

"Winter's for fixing things. Spring's for finding out if anybody remembers where you are," he says.

He's open through Christmas Eve and closed Christmas Day. "Even the fish get a day off," he says.

item.title: Flour Bluff man who filmed lights over air station welcomes Navy review
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Jaime Ortega posted some of the first videos of lights over NAS Corpus Christi after Rafael. He still doesn't know what he saw, and he's glad someone is asking.
item.content:encoded:
Jaime Ortega still has the clips. Lights hanging over NAS Corpus Christi, the nights right after Hurricane Rafael. He pulls them up again Sunday night, after the Navy says it is reviewing security at its Texas air stations.

The Navy ordered the review citing drone reports and the October attack in the ship channel. Ortega's videos were among the first posted.

"I'm an amateur. I point a camera at Jupiter," says Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer who lives in Flour Bluff. "I never said I knew what they were. I said they weren't stars and they weren't planes. I'm glad somebody with more than a backyard telescope is looking."

In September, the station said it was aware of drone reports and working with authorities, and that operations were not affected. The FBI confirmed it was investigating. Reports of new sightings stopped after about ten days.

Ortega says he hasn't filmed anything unusual over the base since then. He still sets up his tripod on clear nights, mostly for Jupiter and Saturn, and the neighbors still ask him about it.

Ortega says his phone blew up after the videos spread. Some messages were thoughtful. Some were not.

"People wanted me to say it was aliens, or the end of the world," he says. "It was lights. That's what I filmed. I'm not going to make it bigger than it is."

The Navy isn't discussing what the review will cover. Ortega has his own advice for anyone who sees something strange near the base.

"Write down the time. Note which way it moved. Call it in," he says. "Then post it, if you want. In that order."

item.title: Door-to-door aid teams are coming. Put your papers in one envelope before the knock
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Registration teams are headed to low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Here's what to have ready, what renters can use as proof and how to help a neighbor get set.
item.content:encoded:
Door-to-door aid registration teams are headed to low-income neighborhoods in the surge zone, and you can make that visit shorter by getting your papers together now.

Nueces County and FEMA announced the visits Wednesday, two days after an analysis by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi researcher found those neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. The county has not released a schedule.

One envelope, by the door: Your ID and the Social Security numbers of the people in your home. A working phone number, even a borrowed one, where FEMA can call you back. Insurance papers if you have coverage. Photos of the damage, printed or on your phone.

Renters: FEMA needs to see that you lived at the address. A lease works. If yours is missing, handwritten or wrong, gather backups with your name and address on them, such as a utility bill, a pay stub or a letter from your child's school or your employer.

Already applied? You don't need to start over. Put your registration number and any FEMA letters in the envelope too.

"The more you have in your hand when the team gets there, the shorter the visit and the fewer follow-up letters," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6.

Is it really them? As Harborline 6 reported Wednesday, team members carry federal photo ID and never charge a fee. Nobody needs your password.

"If your neighbor doesn't have a phone or a car, help them fill their envelope this weekend," said Dwayne Pruitt, spokesman for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Then tell them a team is coming, so they open the door."

Harborline 6 will post the visit schedule on our live blog as soon as the county releases it.

item.title: Aid teams knocking? How to tell a real registration team from a scam
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The county and FEMA say registration teams will go door to door in low-income surge-zone neighborhoods. Here's how to make sure the person at your door is legitimate.
item.content:encoded:
Aid registration is coming to your front door. Here's how to make sure the person knocking is the real thing.

County and FEMA officials announced Wednesday that registration teams will go door to door in low-income neighborhoods in Hurricane Rafael's storm surge zone. The move comes two days after an analysis found those neighborhoods received aid dollars at about half their share of residents.

"Every one of our people will have federal photo ID, and none of them will charge you a fee," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "If you're not sure, ask to see the badge, and call the helpline to check."

How to spot a real team:

They show federal photo identification.

They never ask for money. Applying for FEMA aid is free.

They never ask for your bank PIN or your account passwords.

They don't pressure you to sign anything on the spot.

Red flags:

Someone asks for a fee to "speed up" your application.

Someone asks for your FEMA account password. FEMA said last month that 410 applicant accounts were taken over by attackers using passwords stolen from other sites, and it added extra verification after that.

Someone sends you a link by text instead of pointing you to the official FEMA website or app.

If something feels wrong, close the door and call the FEMA helpline or local police.

Already applied? You don't need to apply again; your status and deposit details are on FEMA's official website or app.

Haven't applied? Registration remains open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.

item.title: "We told them in September": neighbors react to analysis showing an aid gap
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: A church relief hub leader and a North Beach resident say the finding that low-income surge-zone neighborhoods got about half their share of aid matches what they lived through.
item.content:encoded:
Pastor Gloria Whitfield doesn't need a spreadsheet to know who got help after Hurricane Rafael. She has a sign-in sheet.

"We told them in September. We told them in October," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall since the storm. "Now there's a study, and everybody's surprised. I'm not surprised. I'm tired."

An analysis released Monday by Coastline Public Radio and a Texas A&M-Corpus Christi researcher found low-income neighborhoods in the storm surge zone received aid dollars at about half their share of residents. In those neighborhoods, the median 911 response time ran 2.1 times that of high-income areas.

Whitfield's hub handed out food and water in the first days after the storm, before official distribution reached some neighborhoods near the bay.

On North Beach, Marcus Bell, 67, remembers the days when the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway were closed and his neighborhood was cut off from downtown.

"When the bridges closed, you were on your own. Nobody was getting to us fast," said Bell, a retired welder. "I had neighbors who never even tried to call."

The analysis didn't determine the causes of the gap, and the researcher behind it says that's the next question.

What you can do:

If you haven't registered for FEMA individual assistance, registration is still open for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.

If you don't have a phone or internet, church and neighborhood hubs have been helping neighbors apply.

If you already applied and have questions about your status, FEMA's helpline can help.

Harborline 6 will keep following the response to the findings.

item.title: Geminid meteor shower peaks Monday night: a Flour Bluff skywatcher's tips
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Jaime Ortega, whose videos of lights over the air station drew attention in September, says this week's show is the real thing, and easy to explain.
item.content:encoded:
Jaime Ortega has his folding chair, his thermos and his tripod ready for Monday night.

The Geminid meteor shower, one of the best of the year, peaks Monday night into early Tuesday. Under dark skies, patient watchers can see dozens of meteors an hour, though this year a full moon will wash out the fainter ones.

"This one's easy. It's little bits of rock burning up," said Ortega, 42, a hobby astronomer in Flour Bluff. "No mystery. Just get away from the streetlights and give your eyes twenty minutes."

Ortega knows something about mysterious lights. In September, he posted videos of lights hovering over Naval Air Station Corpus Christi at night. At the time, the station said it knew of the drone reports and was working with authorities; the FBI confirmed an investigation. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.

"I haven't filmed anything like that since," Ortega said. "I still look. Most of what people send me now is planes, satellites and Venus. That's fine. Keep sending it."

Tips for watching:

Start after 10 p.m. The show usually gets better after midnight.

Get away from city lights. A dark beach or a rural road works, but follow posted hours and don't park on the shoulder.

Lie back and look at a wide patch of sky. You don't need a telescope or binoculars.

Dress warm. The breeze off the bay gets cold after dark in December.

Put your phone away. The screen ruins your night vision.

Ortega plans to film the shower and post the best streaks. "If anybody sees something that isn't a meteor, tell me," he said. "I'll tell you what it probably is. I'm careful with the word 'probably.'"

Check the Harborline 6 forecast before you head out. Clouds could get in the way.

item.title: Christmas lights over blue tarps: a Calallen block decorates storm-damaged homes
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Neighbors on Leticia Ramos's street are stringing lights on houses still waiting for roof repairs. Before you plug in, here's how to do it safely.
item.content:encoded:
The tarps are still on. The lights are going up anyway.

On Leticia Ramos's block in Calallen, several houses still wear blue tarps from Hurricane Rafael. This week, neighbors started wrapping them in Christmas lights.

"We spent the fall hauling water jugs up and down this street," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who organized neighbors' water runs during the boil-water notice. "This December, we're hauling extension cords. It's a contest now. I'm losing."

Rafael made landfall Sept. 14. The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant near Calallen lost both power feeds early in the storm, and the city spent five weeks under a boil-water notice before it was lifted Oct. 23. Some roofs on the block are still waiting on repairs.

Ramos's students made paper snowflakes for her front window. A neighbor set a light-up pelican on top of a tarp. Another strung lights along a fence still leaning from the wind. The lights come on at dusk, and kids from nearby streets have started walking over to see them.

"It's not about pretending it didn't happen," Ramos said. "It's about saying we're still here."

Before you plug in:

If storm water reached your outlets, wiring or breaker box, have an electrician check them first.

Use lights and extension cords rated for outdoor use.

Don't staple or nail lights through a tarp. That's how water gets in.

Don't overload outlets, and turn the lights off when you go to bed.

Keep cords out of puddles and away from downspouts.

Harborline 6 wants to see your lights. Send your photos through the Harborline 6 app.

item.title: Federal watchdog to review Coastal Bend storm contracts
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: A federal inspector general is reviewing emergency debris and fuel contracts awarded after Hurricane Rafael. Here's the background, and what it means for you.
item.content:encoded:
A federal watchdog is now looking at emergency contracts signed after Hurricane Rafael.

A federal inspector general has opened a review of emergency debris and fuel contracts in the Coastal Bend, the Bayside Ledger reported Tuesday. It's not yet clear which contracts are included or how long the review will take. The review adds federal scrutiny to contracts signed in the first weeks after Hurricane Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, when agencies moved fast to clear roads and restore services.

Here's the background:

Debris: The county awarded a $14.2 million sole-source debris contract to Vantorra Restoration in September. Records obtained by the Ledger show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated. The county paused payments Friday pending an audit. Vantorra denies overbilling, and its managing partner told the Ledger the company has nothing to hide.

Fuel: In a separate case, the Navy suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, on Nov. 28 pending a fuel quality review tied to the station's October generator failure. Quellmar says its fuel meets specifications and that it will cooperate fully with any review.

What's an inspector general? An independent office inside a federal agency that audits and investigates how federal money is spent. A review is not a criminal charge and not a finding of wrongdoing.

What it means for you: Nothing changes for residents today. The county has not announced any change to debris pickup, and questions about debris on your street still go to the county.

Harborline 6 will follow the review and update this story.

item.title: Fact check: The county's pause on debris payments doesn't freeze FEMA aid, and no audit has found theft
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Posts about the county's decision to pause payments to its debris contractor are spreading with two false claims attached.
item.content:encoded:
Posts about the county's pause on payments to its debris contractor are spreading with two false claims attached. Here's what's true and what isn't.

WHAT'S TRUE: The county paused payments to Vantorra Restoration on Friday pending an audit. The pause followed a Bayside Ledger report that records show the company billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra denies overbilling.

CLAIM: "Your FEMA money is frozen too." FALSE. The pause applies to payments under the county's debris contract. FEMA individual assistance to households is a separate federal program, and registration remains open in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.

CLAIM: "The audit already proved they stole millions." FALSE. The audit has not been completed, and no findings have been released. The county has not accused the company of wrongdoing.

"There are no findings yet," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "When there are, you'll hear them from us, not from a meme."

This is the third set of claims Harborline 6 has checked since a wave of posts about contractors and aid began Nov. 28. Fact-checkers have found that some questions about emergency contracts are legitimate. The specific posts checked here are not.

How to check a claim yourself: look for a source document, check the date and compare any number with public records.

Questions about your own FEMA application go to FEMA's helpline or official website. Questions about debris pickup still go to the county.

item.title: County halts payments to debris contractor while it audits the bills
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The county says the pause on payments to Vantorra Restoration is "not a finding of anything." The company denies overbilling.
item.content:encoded:
The county is putting payments to its hurricane debris contractor on hold.

County officials say payments to Vantorra Restoration are paused pending an audit. The move comes two days after the Bayside Ledger reported records showing Vantorra billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated.

"We're not accusing anybody of anything today," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "We're doing the math before we write the next check. That's what you'd do with your own money, and this is your money."

Rafael made landfall Sept. 14, and debris lined streets across the region for weeks. Vantorra holds a $14.2 million emergency debris contract that the county awarded without competitive bidding ten days later. The company has denied overbilling, and its managing partner, Derek Sloane, has said the county's surveys undercount the debris his crews haul.

The records the Ledger obtained show the gap, not the reason for it. A survey estimate is not a count, and an invoice is the contractor's own tally of what it hauled.

How long will the audit take? The county hasn't said.

What it means for you: The county has not announced any change to debris pickup. Questions about debris on your street still go to the county.

Watch what you share: The pause is not a finding of wrongdoing, and no audit results have been released. Harborline 6 has already seen posts claiming otherwise.

Harborline 6 will update this story as the audit moves forward.

item.title: Fact check: The debris billing report is real, but it doesn't show "stolen aid checks"
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Viral posts are stretching a Bayside Ledger investigation into claims it doesn't support. Here is what the records show, and what they don't.
item.content:encoded:
A real news report is being stretched into a false claim.

WHAT'S TRUE: The Bayside Ledger obtained records showing Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage estimated by the county's own drone and satellite surveys. The company denies overbilling. Vantorra holds a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract with the county.

CLAIM: "The debris company billed 2.3 times its contract." MISLEADING. The 2.3 figure compares tons billed with tons the surveys estimated. It does not compare dollars billed with the $14.2 million contract value, and the Ledger did not report how much the company has been paid.

CLAIM: "This proves contractors stole your FEMA check." NO EVIDENCE. The Ledger's report concerns billing for debris removal under a county contract. It says nothing about FEMA payments to individual households, and the posts offer no evidence for that claim.

One post from @CoastTruthTX reads: "SEE?? We TOLD you. They are stealing YOUR aid." The account previously spread false claims that the military was seizing homes after landfall.

Fact-checkers have said since the rumor wave began Nov. 28 that some questions about emergency contracts are legitimate. The Ledger's records are exactly that kind of question. The posts built on top of them are not.

How to check a claim yourself: find the original report, read past the headline and compare any number in a post with the number in the source.

If you're worried about your own aid: Log in to your FEMA account through the official website or app and check your application status and deposit details. Questions about debris pickup go to the county.

item.title: Debris contractor denies overbilling after report finds billed tonnage at 2.3 times county estimates
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Records obtained by the Bayside Ledger show Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's surveys estimated. The company says it bills for what it hauls.
item.content:encoded:
The company hired to haul away Hurricane Rafael's debris is pushing back today after a newspaper investigation raised questions about its bills.

Records obtained by the Bayside Ledger show Vantorra Restoration billed for about 2.3 times the debris tonnage the county's own drone and satellite surveys estimated. Vantorra holds a $14.2 million emergency debris contract that the county awarded without competitive bidding in September, as debris blocked streets across the region.

Vantorra managing partner Derek Sloane denies overbilling. "I've got trucks, I've got drivers, and I've got a ticket for every load," Sloane told Harborline 6 by phone. "We've been working around the clock for these folks since the water went down. Come count 'em with me."

The records do not show why the two figures differ. Survey estimates are not exact counts, and invoices reflect what a contractor says it hauled.

Emergency rules allow contracts to be awarded without bidding when delays would endanger the public, but those contracts usually get a closer look once the emergency passes.

County emergency management spokesman Dwayne Pruitt said the county is reviewing the records and would not comment further today. The Ledger said it shared its findings with Vantorra before publishing.

What this means for you: The county has not announced any change to debris pickup. If debris is still sitting at your curb, contact the county with pickup questions.

What's next: The Ledger says it has requested more records on the contract, including payments to date. Harborline 6 will follow the county's response and update this story.

item.title: Giving Tuesday: how to make sure your storm donation reaches Coastal Bend neighbors
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Relief groups say needs remain ten weeks after Hurricane Rafael. A freight manager who moved relief cargo explains why cash goes further, and how to give safely.
item.content:encoded:
Tomorrow is Giving Tuesday. On the Coastal Bend, the need hasn't gone anywhere.

Church and neighborhood hubs have handed out food and water since the first days after Hurricane Rafael, sometimes before official distribution reached their streets. Many are still running ten weeks later.

Terry Akins knows what it takes to move donated goods. His company, Gulf Relief Logistics, handled 40 relief containers that waited out the anchorage backlog for weeks before the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider finally berthed in October, about a month late.

"Stuff is heavy. Money moves at the speed of light," said Akins, the company's regional manager. "A pallet of water somebody collected three states away is a lot of diesel and a lot of forklift time before it gets here. Give money to people who are already here."

Before you give:

Give to groups you know, like a local church, food bank or school.

Type the web address yourself. Don't tap a link in a text or social media post.

Be wary of anyone who wants payment by gift card, wire transfer or cryptocurrency.

Watch out for lookalike sites that copy the names of real charities or agencies.

Ask what your money will buy. A good local group can tell you.

If you applied for FEMA aid yourself, check your own account, too. Last week FEMA said 410 applicant accounts were hijacked with passwords stolen from other sites. Affected applicants will be repaid, the agency says. FEMA never charges a fee to apply.

"The stuff that helps most right now is boring," Akins said. "Diapers, cleaning supplies, grocery cards. Nobody takes a picture of a grocery card. It still feeds a family."

item.title: Fact check: No, the county's debris contract isn't $140 million, and FEMA hasn't stopped paying families
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: A new wave of posts claims contractors are "stealing aid." Some questions about emergency contracts are fair. These specific claims are false.
item.content:encoded:
A new wave of viral posts claims contractors are stealing hurricane aid from Coastal Bend families. Harborline 6 checked the most-shared claims. Some questions about emergency contracts are legitimate. These specific posts are false.

CLAIM: The county handed a debris company $140 million. FALSE. The county awarded a $14.2 million sole-source emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC on Sept. 24, according to public records. The $140 million figure appears in posts with no source.

CLAIM: FEMA stopped paying families so the money could go to contractors. FALSE. FEMA individual assistance registration remains open in Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Aid to households and county cleanup contracts are paid through separate programs.

One widely shared post from @CoastTruthTX, an account that spread false claims after landfall that the military was seizing homes, reads: "THEY GOT RICH OFF OUR STORM. Contractors are STEALING your aid and nobody will say it." The post offers no evidence.

WHAT'S FAIR TO ASK: The debris contract was awarded without competitive bidding, and news organizations including the Bayside Ledger have requested records on emergency contracts. Separately, the Navy said Sunday it has suspended Quellmar Fuel Partners, the emergency fuel supplier for Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, pending a fuel quality review. The company says its fuel meets specifications. Those questions have answers still to come.

"Ask us about any contract. The records are public, and you'll get an answer," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "What I'm asking is, check before you share. A made-up number doesn't hold anybody accountable."

Before you share: look for a source document, check the date and be wary of all-caps posts that say nobody else will report something.

item.title: FEMA: 410 aid accounts taken over in automated login attack; victims will be repaid
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Attackers made about 220,000 login attempts using passwords stolen from other sites, FEMA says. The agency has added extra verification.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA says 410 disaster-aid applicant accounts were taken over after about 220,000 automated login attempts, and applicants who were affected will be repaid.

The attempts used usernames and passwords stolen from other sites, according to the agency, and some of them worked. FEMA said Wednesday it has added extra verification to applicant accounts.

"If your account was one of them, you will be repaid," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We've added verification, and we're asking everyone to check their deposit information today, even if you think you're fine."

The announcement comes a week after some Coastal Bend applicants reported that their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge, and five days after FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some accounts. Harborline 6 reported Tuesday on how to check your deposit details.

FEMA did not say how much money was redirected or who was behind the login attempts. Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.

What changes for you:

The advice to confirm your bank details on FEMA's official website or app still stands.

If the password on your FEMA account is one you've used anywhere else, change it now. Start with your email account, because whoever controls your email can reset everything else.

Spot something off? FEMA and your bank both need to hear about it.

No internet access? The FEMA helpline or a recovery center can help you check your information.

Heading out of town for Thanksgiving? Do it before you go.

Harborline 6 will update this story as FEMA releases more information.

item.title: Applied for FEMA aid? Check your deposit details before the holiday
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: FEMA says some applicant accounts were accessed without permission. Here is how to check yours, and what to do if something looks wrong.
item.content:encoded:
If you applied for FEMA disaster aid after Hurricane Rafael, take five minutes before Thanksgiving to check where your money is going.

FEMA confirmed Friday that some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization. That came two days after aid applicants in the Coastal Bend said their direct-deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. The agency is urging every applicant to verify their deposit information now.

"Log in, look at your bank details, and if anything is off, call us right away," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Don't wait for a payment to go missing to find out."

Harborline 6's step-by-step guide from Saturday has the details. The five-minute version:

Open FEMA's site or app yourself, not from a link someone sent you, and sign in.

Find your payment details and hold them up against a check or your banking app.

See numbers you didn't enter? Call the FEMA helpline and your bank that day.

Last, swap your password for one you've never used anywhere else.

Ostrander said FEMA never charges a fee to apply and will never call to ask for your password. "If someone calls asking for it, hang up," she said. "That's not us."

No internet at home? A recovery center or a trusted neighbor can help you check. Don't share your password with anyone who helps you, and sign out when you're done.

Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, and recovery centers have seen long lines since. Harborline 6 is following this story and will update it as FEMA releases more information.

item.title: Step by step: how to check and fix your FEMA deposit information
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: FEMA confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts. Here's exactly what to do, and what to do if you don't have a computer.
item.content:encoded:
Some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, FEMA says, so every applicant should make sure their direct-deposit information is right. Here's how, step by step.

Step 1: Get to the real site. Open your phone or computer's web browser and type FEMA's official website address yourself. Don't tap a link in a text, email or social media post, even if it looks official.

Step 2: Sign in. If you can't remember your password, use the official reset option on the site. Don't ask a stranger to sign in for you.

Step 3: Find your payment information. Look for the section that shows how you'll be paid. Compare the bank routing and account numbers to a check, a bank statement or your bank's app.

Step 4: If it's wrong, call. Call FEMA's helpline right away and say your direct-deposit information was changed without your permission. Write down the date, time and name of the person you talk to.

Step 5: Call your bank. Tell them what happened.

Step 6: Lock it down. Change your password to one you don't use anywhere else. Turn on extra sign-in protection if it's offered.

No computer? Call FEMA's helpline, or go to a disaster recovery center and ask staff to help you check. Many church and neighborhood hubs have volunteers helping people log in.

Red flags: FEMA will never call, text or email asking for your password, and it never charges a fee. "If it isn't us, hang up and call us," says Rachel Ostrander of FEMA Region 6.

FEMA has not said how many accounts were affected. Harborline 6 will update you when it does.

item.title: FEMA confirms unauthorized access to some aid applicant accounts; check your deposit info now
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: FEMA says some applicant accounts were accessed without authorization and urges every applicant to verify their direct-deposit details.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA confirms that some disaster aid applicant accounts were accessed without authorization, and it is urging applicants to verify their direct-deposit information.

"We have confirmed unauthorized access to some applicant accounts," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "We are urging every applicant to log in and verify their direct-deposit information today. If anything looks wrong, call our helpline right away. We will help you correct it."

FEMA does not say how many accounts were affected, how they were accessed, or whether any payments went to changed accounts. Ostrander says FEMA will share more when it can.

The confirmation comes two days after Harborline 6 reported that some applicants in Nueces County said their deposit details had been changed without their knowledge. Registration for individual assistance opened Nov. 13 for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties.

If you applied, here's the short version:

Type FEMA's official web address into your browser. A link in a text or email could take you somewhere else.

Look at the bank account where your aid will be deposited. Not yours? Call FEMA's helpline, and keep a note of when you called and who answered.

Let your bank know, too.

Pick a new FEMA password you've never used anywhere else, and switch on extra sign-in protection if the site offers it.

Watch out for scams. FEMA will never call, text or email asking for your password or a fee. "If someone contacts you claiming to be from FEMA and asks for money or your login, hang up and call us," Ostrander says.

Harborline 6 will keep following this story.

item.title: Some FEMA applicants say their deposit details were changed without their knowledge
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Harborline 6 has heard from aid applicants who logged in and found bank information they did not enter. Here's how to check yours right now.
item.content:encoded:
Some people who applied for federal disaster aid after Hurricane Rafael say the direct-deposit details on their applications were changed without their knowledge.

Harborline 6 has heard from several applicants in Nueces County who say they logged in to check on their applications this week and found a bank account number they did not recognize. A Flour Bluff woman who asked not to be named says she registered by phone on the first day, entered her credit union account, and on Tuesday saw a different bank listed. "I didn't change anything," she says. "I didn't even know you could."

FEMA opened individual assistance registration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties on Saturday, Nov. 13. Harborline 6 asked FEMA about the reports Wednesday morning. The agency had not responded by midday.

Harborline 6 has not independently confirmed how the changes happened, and it is not known how many applicants are affected.

What to do right now:

Log in to your FEMA account only through FEMA's official website. Type the address yourself. Do not use a link from a text or email.

Check your direct-deposit information. If it is not your account, call FEMA's helpline right away and say your deposit information was changed without your permission. Write down the date, time and the name of the person you speak with.

Call your own bank and let them know.

Change your password, and don't use the same password you use on other sites.

If you have seen a change you didn't make, Harborline 6 wants to hear from you. We will update this story when FEMA responds.

item.title: Filing a spill damage claim? Here's your checklist
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Fishers and shoreline businesses that lost income to the September oil spill can now file. Here's what to gather and how to protect yourself.
item.content:encoded:
The claims center run for the tankers' owners begins taking lost-income claims this week from commercial fishers and shoreline businesses hurt by the oil spill in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, as federal oil spill law requires. If a claim sits unpaid for 90 days, you can take it to the Coast Guard's National Pollution Funds Center.

"Start the claim, then keep adding to it," says Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Nobody expects you to have it all on day one."

Who can file: Commercial fishers who lost income because of the spill and the fishing closure in the bays, and shoreline businesses that lost income. Oil damage to shoreline property? That part of the center opened in September.

If you fish for a living, gather: Your fishing licenses and boat registration. Trip logs or trip tickets showing what you caught before the spill. Tax returns or other records showing your income in past seasons. Receipts for fuel, ice, gear and crew. Any notes on days you could not fish.

If you own shoreline property, gather: Photos of oil on your property, with dates if you have them. Receipts for any cleanup you paid for. Repair estimates. Anything showing what the property looked like before.

Protect yourself: You do not need to pay anyone to file a claim. Be careful with anyone who calls, texts or knocks offering to file for a fee or promising a bigger payout. Do not give out bank information to anyone you did not contact first through official channels.

Still seeing oil? Crews are still monitoring shorelines and marshes. If you see oil, call the state's spill hotline instead of cleaning it up yourself.

Remember: Filing a claim does not reopen the bays. The fishing and shellfish closures stay in effect until Texas Parks and Wildlife and the state health department say otherwise.

item.title: FEMA aid registration opens today: what to bring and how to sign up
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Individual assistance registration opens Saturday for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. Here's what you need before you get in line.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA individual assistance registration opens today for residents of Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties who had damage or losses from Hurricane Rafael.

"Registration is the first step, and it's the most important one," says Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Register even if you're not sure you qualify. If you have insurance, file with your insurance company too. And keep every receipt."

How to register: online through FEMA's official website, by phone through FEMA's helpline, or in person at a disaster recovery center in the three coastal counties. Ostrander says lines at recovery centers may be long on the first days, and phone and online registration are open to everyone.

What to have ready:

Photo ID and your Social Security number. The address of the damaged home and a phone number where FEMA can reach you. Your insurance information, if you have it. A short description of the damage and what you lost. Photos help. Your bank's routing number and your account number if you want payments by direct deposit. Renters: something that shows you lived at the address, like a lease or a utility bill.

Protect yourself: FEMA does not charge to register, and FEMA staff will never ask you for money. Only use FEMA's official website or helpline. "If someone calls you offering to speed up your application for a fee, hang up," Ostrander says.

After the storm, the city warned residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal, and a researcher later linked viral rumor posts to the same lookalike site. If you get a link by text or email, don't click it. Type the official address yourself.

Need help? Many church and neighborhood hubs are helping people register by phone. Bring your documents.

item.title: At the jetties, a tug captain and a bait shop owner watch the ships come back
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Ray Dupree, whose tug was damaged in the Oct. 28 blast, wanted to see the channel open with his own eyes. Bill Hargrove brought a lawn chair.
item.content:encoded:
Ray Dupree stands at the rail on the beach road with his hands in his jacket pockets and watches a tanker slide between the jetties.

"I wanted to see it," says Dupree, 56, master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay. "Two weeks ago I was out there counting heads. Today I'm standing here counting ships. That's better."

Dupree's tug was damaged and two of his crew were hurt when an explosion went off beside it near the jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. The Navy says an explosive device caused the blast. The channel reopened Thursday after a 14-day closure and a full sweep, and on Friday ships are moving steadily through the pass.

His deckhand, Eddie Fontenot, is still recovering. "He called me this morning to ask if it was open," Dupree says. "I told him it was open, and he's not. Not yet."

A few yards down, Bill Hargrove has set up a lawn chair. The owner of Hargrove Bait & Tackle has been selling from a folding table since Rafael gutted his shop in September. "Best seat on the island," he says. "Free, too. Don't tell anybody."

Hargrove, 64, says the island needs the traffic back. "A ship going by doesn't buy bait," he says. "But it means the pass is open, and the pass being open means the people come back. That's how this town works."

At the Port of Corpus Christi, a sealift ship is loading a Fort Hood aviation brigade's helicopters and equipment, which the Army says will sail over the next five days for an overseas rotation.

Dupree says he will be back on the water when the company has a boat for him. "I'll watch the water at the jetties like I always have," he says. "Harder, maybe."

What you need to know: Expect heavy ship traffic in the channel through the weekend as vessels that waited offshore come in.

item.title: Corpus Christi Ship Channel reopens after 14-day closure and full sweep
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The Coast Guard lifts the closure Thursday morning. Exports resume, and ships begin moving through the Port Aransas jetties for the first time since the Oct. 28 blast.
item.content:encoded:
The Corpus Christi Ship Channel is open again.

The Coast Guard reopens the channel Thursday morning after a 14-day closure and a full sweep by Navy teams, ending a shutdown that began with an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Crude exports from the port resume.

"The search is complete, and the Captain of the Port has reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to vessel traffic," says Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We thank the Navy teams and our port partners for their patience and their work. Mariners should follow all directions from the Coast Guard and pilots as traffic resumes."

Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer, says Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams have finished their search. "The channel has been cleared," Moreau says. "Our teams covered every stretch of water they needed to, and they are proud to hand it back to the port."

A second explosive device, found near the entrance last Friday, was rendered safe by Navy teams. Two crew members aboard the tug Corrin Bay were injured in the Oct. 28 blast. The FBI is investigating.

Thursday is Veterans Day, and on the island, people stopped on the beach road to watch the first vessels head for the jetties.

What you need to know: Ship traffic is moving again in the channel. Expect more vessel activity near the jetties and along the waterfront over the next several days as ships waiting offshore come in. Texas Parks and Wildlife's fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill is separate and stays in place.

Harborline 6 will have live coverage from Port Aransas tonight at 6.

item.title: Navy teams find second explosive device near entrance channel, render it safe
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: No one was hurt. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel stays closed while the search continues.
item.content:encoded:
Navy teams have found a second explosive device near the entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel and rendered it safe, the Navy and Coast Guard say Friday.

No one is hurt. The channel remains closed to all traffic.

"Navy teams located a second explosive device near the entrance channel and rendered it safe," says Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a Navy public affairs officer. "No one was injured. The search of the channel continues, and it will continue until we are confident it is complete."

Moreau would not describe the device or where exactly it was found, citing safety and the ongoing investigation.

The find comes eight days after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Oct. 28. Two crew members were hurt in that blast. The Navy has said it was caused by an explosive device, and the FBI is investigating.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi says the closure stays in place. "The channel will reopen when the search is complete and the Captain of the Port is satisfied it is safe," Ruiz says. "We are not giving a date today."

What this means for you: The ship channel is still closed. Crude exports from the port are still halted. There is no change to roads, bridges or beach access announced by officials. If you see something unusual on a beach or in the water, don't touch it. Keep your distance and call 911.

Harborline 6 will update this story as officials release more.

item.title: Port Aransas waits it out as Navy teams search the channel
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Four days after the blast at the jetties, the island is quiet. A bait shop owner who heard it says the waiting is the hard part.
item.content:encoded:
The jetties are quiet Monday. No tankers. No tugs. Just gulls, a stiff north wind and a few people standing on the beach road watching Navy and Coast Guard boats work the channel.

Bill Hargrove has watched that water for most of his 64 years. His shop, Hargrove Bait & Tackle, sits a short walk from the jetties. Rafael gutted it in September, and he is still selling hooks and ice from a folding table while he rebuilds.

He was asleep at home when the blast came around 1 a.m. Thursday. "It wasn't thunder. I know thunder," Hargrove says. "It was one big thump, and then every dog on the island started in. I laid there thinking, well, that's not a storm, so what is it?"

The Navy says the explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay was caused by an explosive device. Two crew members were hurt. Navy teams trained in explosives and mine clearance are working the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.

For the island, the closure lands on top of a storm that already took the fall season. "First the water came in the shop. Then the oil. Now nobody can go in or out of the pass," Hargrove says. "I keep telling people we're open. Open for what, they ask me. Fair question."

He says customers mostly want to talk. "Everybody's got a theory. I tell them I sell bait, not theories."

What you need to know: The ship channel is closed to all traffic until the Coast Guard says otherwise. No reopening date has been announced. Crude exports from the port remain halted. If you see something unusual on a beach or in the water, keep your distance and call 911.

item.title: On a quiet Halloween, Port Aransas waits on the channel
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Kids in costumes, a closed ship channel and Navy and Coast Guard teams searching it. Bill Hargrove's bait shop is open, sort of.
item.content:encoded:
Halloween in Port Aransas. A kid in a shark costume sprints past a bait shop with plywood still nailed over one window. Out past the jetties, Navy and Coast Guard teams keep searching the ship channel.

Bill Hargrove has a folding table out front and a cooler full of bait nobody is buying. "Bay's closed, channel's shut, and I'm in the candy business now," says Hargrove, 64. "Terrible margins."

Hargrove's shop sits near the jetties. The explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay around 1 a.m. Thursday woke him. On Saturday, the Navy said it was caused by an explosive device. Navy teams that clear explosives and mines are out on the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.

"I've lived by these rocks a long time," Hargrove says. "You learn every sound they make. That one wasn't theirs."

Two crew members on the tug were injured. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all vessel traffic, with no word on when it will reopen. Fishing in the bays is still closed after the oil spill.

The town is doing what it did after the storm: getting on with it. Porch lights are on. A few trucks are parked along the beach road. Down the street, a church parking lot is running a trunk-or-treat, candy handed out of pickup beds. A family in matching pirate hats stops at Hargrove's table.

"Arr," says the youngest. Hargrove hands over two candy bars.

"That's the most business I've done all week," he says.

item.title: Fact-check: A foreign state broadcaster mocks the port closure. Here's what officials actually say.
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: A state-run outlet abroad is calling the Corpus Christi channel closure a sign of U.S. weakness. What's confirmed: an explosive device, an active Navy and Coast Guard search, and an FBI investigation.
item.content:encoded:
THE CLAIM: A foreign state broadcaster is airing segments that mock the closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel as a sign of American weakness. One segment called it "a harbor America cannot even keep open."

WHAT'S CONFIRMED: The channel is closed. The Navy said Saturday that Thursday's blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating. Two tug crew members were injured.

WHAT THE BROADCAST LEAVES OUT: Closing a channel after an explosion is a safety decision, and the Coast Guard made it within hours. "Closing the channel is how you keep people safe while you find out what happened," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That's the system working."

WHY IT MATTERS: Misleading posts spread fast after a disaster. Since Hurricane Rafael, false claims about the military seizing homes have circulated locally, and county and base officials have debunked them. Whatever the source, mocking or misleading messages work the same way: they want you angry, and they want you to share.

WHAT TO DO: Don't share clips from foreign state media, even to argue with them; sharing spreads them. Get updates from the Coast Guard, the Navy and local news. Harborline 6 is not naming or linking the outlet. If a clip reaches you, check who made it and when before you react.

item.title: Tug captain on jetty blast: "My first thought was my crew"
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Capt. Ray Dupree, master of the Corrin Bay, speaks for the first time since the overnight explosion that injured two of his crew. The ship channel stays closed.
item.content:encoded:
Capt. Ray Dupree has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. He says nothing prepared him for early Thursday morning.

"You don't expect the water to come up beside you like that," Dupree tells Harborline 6. "It went off close, off our port bow. My first thought was my crew. My second thought was my crew."

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. Around 1 a.m. Thursday, an explosion went off beside the tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The tug is damaged. Two crew members are injured.

Dupree won't talk about their conditions. "That's their business and their families'," he says. "They did everything right. Everybody on that boat did."

He won't guess at a cause, either. "Ask the Coast Guard," he says. "I drive tugs. I'm not going to stand here and tell you something I don't know."

The Coast Guard says the cause is unknown. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all vessel traffic, with no estimate for reopening.

The Corrin Bay is one of the harbor tugs that help guide big ships through the channel and into their berths. It is work Dupree has done most of his adult life, in fog, wind and the dark.

On the waterfront, other boat crews stop by to shake his hand. Dupree nods, says thanks, and keeps it short.

Asked what comes next, he looks out toward the water. "Wait on the Coast Guard. Check on my guys. Then get back to work when they say it's safe," he says. "That's the job."

item.title: Jetty explosion: What we know tonight, and what we don't
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Two tug crew members are hurt, the ship channel is closed and the cause is unknown. Separately, the FAA says reports of GPS interference near Corpus Christi have stopped.
item.content:encoded:
Here's where things stand Thursday night after the explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

WHAT WE KNOW: Around 1 a.m., an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. The tug is damaged. Two crew members are injured. The Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic.

WHERE: The jetties mark the Gulf entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, at the north end of Mustang Island. Every ship going in or out of the port passes between them.

WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: The cause. The Coast Guard says it is unknown and won't speculate. There is no estimate for reopening the channel, and the injured crew members' names and conditions have not been released.

ONLINE: Posts guessing at the cause are circulating. Harborline 6 has not confirmed any of them, and no agency has. If a post claims to know what happened, ask where the information came from before you share it.

SPILL CLEANUP: The Unified Command says cleanup of the Inner Harbor oil spill is moving to a monitoring phase and has lifted inner-channel restrictions. The bays remain closed to fishing. Report oiled wildlife to the hotline.

BOATERS: The ship channel is closed to all vessel traffic. Follow Coast Guard instructions and broadcast notices.

GPS: Separately, the FAA says reports of GPS interference near Corpus Christi have stopped. "We are no longer receiving reports of interference in the area," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Pilots should continue to check notices before every flight."

Harborline 6 will update this story overnight and on air in the morning.

item.title: Explosion near Port Aransas jetties damages tug; two crew hurt; ship channel closed
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The blast happened around 1 a.m. beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay. The Coast Guard has closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. The cause is unknown.
item.content:encoded:
An explosion goes off beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties overnight. Two crew members are hurt. The Coast Guard has closed the ship channel.

It happens around 1 a.m. The tug is the Corrin Bay. The Coast Guard says the tug is damaged and two of its crew are injured. Their names and conditions have not been released.

"At approximately 1 a.m., the Coast Guard received a report of an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties involving the harbor tug Corrin Bay," says Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Two crew members were injured. No vessel will move in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel until further notice. The cause is unknown, and we will not speculate."

The jetties mark the Gulf entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, the route every ship takes in and out of the port.

WHAT WE KNOW: An explosion. A damaged tug. Two injured crew members. A closed channel.

WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: What caused it. How badly the tug is damaged. When the channel will reopen.

BOATERS: The channel is closed to all vessel traffic. Stay off the water near the jetties and follow Coast Guard instructions.

Harborline 6 is hearing from Port Aransas residents who say a loud boom woke them. If you need help, call 911. Otherwise, please keep the lines clear.

The channel partly reopened two weeks ago after a month-long closure for Hurricane Rafael. Tonight, nothing is moving through it.

Harborline 6 is headed to Port Aransas. Refresh this page for updates.

item.title: Relief airlift at NAS Corpus Christi wraps up this week
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The last of 40 relief flights are due at the air station. The FAA's GPS interference notice for the Corpus Christi area remains in place.
item.content:encoded:
The relief airlift into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is in its final days. Twenty-six military C-17s and 14 civilian charters were scheduled to land over ten days starting Oct. 18.

"We're proud the air station could support this effort for our neighbors," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "Thank you to everyone in Flour Bluff and on the south side for putting up with the noise."

The flights kept coming despite reports of GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi. The FAA issued a notice to pilots Saturday, and relief crews have been flying with backup navigation. That notice remains in place.

For neighbors who spent ten days watching big gray jets line up over the bay, the quiet will take some getting used to. Hale said the station would let the community know when the last flight is down.

YOUR WEEK IN RECOVERY:

WATER: The city lifted the boil-water notice Saturday after 35 days. If you haven't flushed your pipes, tossed old ice and replaced fridge filters, do it now.

AIR STATION: A backup generator at NAS Corpus Christi failed during a power interruption. Power is restored, and the cause is under review.

PORT: The ship channel is partly open. The inner channel remains restricted for spill decontamination.

RELIEF CARGO: The 40 relief containers from MV Gulf Provider came ashore Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog.

Have a question about recovery? Send it to Harborline 6, and we'll chase down the answer.

item.title: NAS Corpus Christi backup generator fails during outage; power restored
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The Navy says the cause of the failure is under review. Power is back on at the air station.
item.content:encoded:
A backup generator at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi failed during a power interruption, the Navy says. Power is back on. The cause is under review.

"Power has been restored," says Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "We're reviewing the generator failure and will share what we can when that review is complete."

The station says the interruption happened over the weekend, but it isn't saying how long it lasted or which buildings went dark.

Backup generators are supposed to start automatically when grid power drops, keeping essential systems running until the lights come back. Why this one didn't do its job is the question the review will try to answer.

Harborline 6 asked whether the outage affected the relief airlift that has been landing at the station this month. Hale says the station will share more once the review is done.

The airlift, 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters over ten days, began Oct. 18 and is scheduled to wrap up this week.

It has been a busy stretch for the station. Training aircraft that flew to Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael came home after the storm, and the Army depot that shares the base has been repairing storm damage to its hangars.

Off base, the weekend brought better news. The city lifted its citywide boil-water notice Saturday after 35 days; Districts 3 and 4 remain under their separate notice. If you haven't yet, run your cold-water taps for a few minutes, toss old ice and swap out fridge filters.

Harborline 6 will update this story when the Navy releases the results of its review.

item.title: FAA warns pilots of GPS interference near Corpus Christi; relief flights continue
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of the city. The FAA issued a notice, and relief flights into NAS Corpus Christi are using backup navigation.
item.content:encoded:
Pilots flying near Corpus Christi are reporting GPS interference, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice warning aircraft in the area.

WHAT WE KNOW: The reports cover an area within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, the FAA says. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi are continuing, using backup navigation.

"Pilots operating in the area should be prepared for unreliable GPS signals and use other means of navigation as needed," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "If you experience interference, report it to air traffic control."

"The relief flights are continuing safely," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "Our aircrews and the relief crews train for this, and they're flying with backup navigation. No impact to the relief mission."

WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: What's causing it. Neither the FAA nor the Navy has said where the interference is coming from, and neither would speculate when Harborline 6 asked.

WHAT PILOTS SHOULD DO: Check the FAA notice before every flight, brief your backup navigation, and report anything unusual to air traffic control. That goes for private and student pilots at local airports too, not just the relief crews.

WHAT ABOUT MY PHONE? The FAA notice is for aviation. If you notice problems with a navigation app in your car, Harborline 6 wants to hear about it. Tell us where and when.

THE AIRLIFT: Twenty-six military C-17s and 14 civilian charters are scheduled to land at the air station over ten days. The flights began Monday and have continued through the week.

item.title: Pump parts are here. Here's why you still need to boil your water.
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Replacement parts arrived at the O.N. Stevens plant today, but the notice doesn't lift until installation and testing are done. What to do in the meantime.
item.content:encoded:
Good news, with an asterisk. Replacement pump parts arrived today at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant. The citywide boil-water notice is still in effect.

WHY THE WAIT? The parts have to be installed and the system tested before the city can lift the notice, the water utility says. "Parts on the dock are not the same as safe water at your tap," utility spokesperson Teresa Gallegos told Harborline 6. "We'll lift the notice when the testing says we can, and not an hour before."

WHAT TO DO NOW: Keep boiling tap water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and making ice. Bring it to a rolling boil for two minutes and let it cool. Use boiled or bottled water for baby formula.

HOW WILL I KNOW? Harborline 6 will send an alert and update this page as soon as the city announces a change. Be wary of posts claiming the notice has been lifted before the city says so. Screenshots are not announcements.

WHAT HAPPENED: Hurricane Rafael knocked out both power feeds to the plant early in the storm and damaged its pumps. The plant has been running on temporary pumps with limited capacity. Replacement parts were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded and shipments had to come from out of state.

ALSO TODAY: The relief airlift continues at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, where 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters are scheduled to land over ten days. Expect aircraft noise in Flour Bluff and on the south side.

item.title: Flour Bluff watches the relief airlift roll in
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Big gray cargo jets are landing at NAS Corpus Christi on day two of a ten-day relief airlift. A neighbor with a camera is filming every one he can.
item.content:encoded:
A C-17 drops out of a clear evening sky over Flour Bluff. The rumble rolls across the neighborhood. Jaime Ortega lifts his camera.

"I've honestly lost count," Ortega says, laughing. "It's a lot of airplane."

It's day two of the relief airlift into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. Twenty-six military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters are scheduled to land over ten days, bringing relief supplies to a Coastal Bend still recovering from Hurricane Rafael.

Ortega, 42, is a hobby astronomer who films the night sky from his backyard. After the storm, he was among the residents who posted videos of lights hovering over the air station at night. The station said it was aware of the reports and working with authorities, and the FBI confirmed it was investigating. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.

These lights, he says, are the easy kind. "These ones have a schedule and a reason," Ortega says. "I like that better."

The airlift began Monday, a day after the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider finally unloaded 40 containers at the port. Help is coming in by sea and by air now, and Flour Bluff has a front-row seat.

Down the block, two kids on bikes stop to point as the big jet rolls out on the runway. A neighbor waves a dish towel from her porch. Nobody seems to mind the noise.

"After the storm, everything felt like it was happening to us," Ortega says. "This feels like something happening for us. Somebody should film that part too."

item.title: Relief ship Gulf Provider finally docks with 40 containers
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The cargo ship waited weeks in the offshore backlog. Its relief containers are coming off at the Port of Corpus Christi this morning.
item.content:encoded:
MV Gulf Provider is alongside. After weeks in the offshore anchorage line, the relief cargo ship is at a berth at the Port of Corpus Christi this morning. Its 40 relief containers are coming off.

Cranes swing. Trucks idle in a line along the dock road. A worker in a hard hat waves them forward, one at a time.

The containers were booked five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall. Then the Coast Guard closed the ship channel ahead of the storm, and the ship ended up in the queue offshore. For a cargo ship, that is a long time to sit within sight of the coast. The channel partly reopened Thursday, but the anchorage backlog kept Gulf Provider waiting until now.

"It's about a month later than anybody wanted," says Javier Salinas, spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "But it's here, it's moving, and the channel is doing what it's supposed to do. We're glad to see these boxes on the dock."
