What's inside? The port describes the cargo as relief supplies. Harborline 6 is asking relief agencies where it will be distributed and will update this story.

The wait was part of a bigger backlog. Two days before landfall, when the port closed to inbound traffic, 14 vessels were left holding at the offshore anchorage, and crude exports stopped with them.

Waiting on help? Check with your neighborhood hub or relief agency for updated distribution hours this week.

The inner ship channel is still restricted for spill decontamination. The citywide boil-water notice remains in effect.

item.title: Weekend checklist: Boil-water notice still on, and don't click that "aid portal" link
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Pump parts for the city's water plant are still on the way, so keep boiling. And if a message sends you to a disaster-aid site, check the address first.
item.content:encoded:
It's Saturday, and the citywide boil-water notice is still in effect. Here's what you need to know this weekend.

WATER: Boil tap water before you drink it, cook with it, brush your teeth with it or make ice. Bring it to a rolling boil for two minutes. The notice has been in place since Sept. 18, four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. The O.N. Stevens plant is running on temporary pumps that limit capacity while it waits for replacement parts, which were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded.

"We know how long this has gone on, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, spokesperson for the city water utility. "The notice stays until the plant is repaired and testing shows the water is safe. Please keep boiling."

PHISHING: The city has warned about emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. A threat researcher later found that coordinated rumor posts were linking to the same lookalike site used in those emails, aid-help-portal.example. Never enter personal or banking details on a site you reached through an unsolicited link. Type official addresses yourself.

RUMORS: Posts claiming the military is seizing homes are false, county and base officials have said. Claims that aid is going only to wealthy neighborhoods are false too. If a post makes you angry or scared and asks you to click, slow down and check it first.

PORT: The ship channel partly reopened Thursday. The inner channel remains restricted for spill decontamination, so expect ship traffic to move slowly for a while.

item.title: Recovery checklist: what's still closed and what's changed, a month after Rafael
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The boil-water notice, the bay fishing closure and the ship channel closure are still in place. Here's where things stand and what to do.
item.content:encoded:
It's been almost a month since Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island on Sept. 14. Here's where things stand as of Wednesday.

Water: STILL BOIL. The Sept. 18 citywide boil-water notice has not been lifted. Replacement parts for the O.N. Stevens plant's damaged pumps are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded, and they're shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice.

Stomach illness: EASING. ER visits eased in late September after a surge. Keep up the handwashing, with soap and boiled or bottled water.

Bay fishing: CLOSED. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stays in place. Don't fish or harvest there, and avoid any oil on shorelines.

Ship channel: CLOSED. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Sept. 13, and crude exports are halted. No reopening date has been announced.

Spill investigation: ONGOING. The Coast Guard says investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers involved in the spill. A maintenance vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused and that it revoked all remote access.

Debris: CONTRACT AWARDED. Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract. Sort piles at the curb, out of the street, and check county channels for routes.

Scams: WATCH OUT. A researcher tied post-storm rumor posts to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, also used in phishing emails. Don't click it.

Lights over the air station: QUIET. No new drone sightings since late September. The FBI's investigation continues.

Share this list with a neighbor who isn't online.

item.title: Port Aransas bait shop owner: 'Down to the studs. Customers next.'
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Four weeks after Rafael gutted his shop near the jetties, Bill Hargrove has bare studs and plenty of stories, but not many customers.
item.content:encoded:
PORT ARANSAS — The sign out front of Hargrove Bait & Tackle still says "OPEN-ISH." Inside, the walls are stripped to the studs, with Bill Hargrove's pencil notes scrawled across the bare wood.

"That's where the freezer goes. That's where the rods go. That's where the photo board goes, once people start catching fish again," Hargrove, 64, says, pointing. "I'm writing it on the wall so I don't forget. At my age, if it's not on the wall, it's not happening."

Hurricane Rafael's surge gutted the shop near the jetties when the storm came ashore Sept. 14. Hargrove spent the next weeks tearing out what the water ruined. Now he's planning how it all goes back, one wall at a time.

What hasn't come back is the crowd. Before the storm, Port Aransas had a strong summer, and bait shops and charters stayed busy. Now the island is quiet. Texas Parks and Wildlife has closed fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays because of the oil spill, and it extended the closure last week.

"People call and ask, 'Bill, is it open?' and I tell them the truth," Hargrove says. "Then they ask about the jetties, and I tell them to check with Parks and Wildlife before they go. I'm a bait man, not a lawyer."

He's been selling ice, tackle and coffee, and listening a lot. "Half my business right now is therapy," he says. "Guy comes in for a pack of hooks and stays forty minutes to tell me about his roof."

He's optimistic, in his way. "The fish are still out there. The jetties are still out there. I'm still out here," he says. "Two out of three ain't bad. Three out of three, give it time."

item.title: Not yet: State asks FEMA for household aid as damage checks lag
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Texas has asked FEMA to add aid for households in three coastal counties. Until FEMA decides, nobody can register. Near the bay, families are waiting.
item.content:encoded:
At Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall, the question comes every day: "Pastora, when can we sign up for FEMA?"

"Not yet," Whitfield, 59, tells them. "Nobody can sign up yet. I'd rather tell you the truth than tell you something nice."

Here's why. Texas has formally asked FEMA to add Individual Assistance, the program that helps households, to the federal disaster declaration for Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties. The declaration issued Sept. 18 covers debris removal and emergency protective measures. Help for families depends on joint damage assessments, and those are moving slowly.

"We've got people trying to look at houses on streets they still can't drive down, and near shorelines where the spill response controls who goes in," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "It's slow because it's big. That's the reason, not an excuse."

Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6, says the agency has the state's request. "When there's a decision, we'll announce it, and we'll tell people plainly how to apply," she says.

A few blocks from the hall, Rosa Elizondo, 38, has a bucket in her hallway catching a drip from the ceiling. A home health aide and mother of three, she rents a duplex near the bay. No car, no savings for repairs. Her landlord says soon.

"People think FEMA is like a store. You go, you ask, you get," Elizondo says. "Nobody told us it's more like the bus. First it has to come."

Advocates say families without savings feel the wait most. Whitfield is starting a new page in her penciled binder for neighbors who will need help applying once aid opens.

What to do now: Take photos of damage before you clean up. Keep every receipt. If you have insurance, file your claim now. And if anyone offers to sign you up for federal aid today, it's a scam.

item.title: That aid website might be fake: how to spot the lookalike before you click
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: A researcher has tied post-storm rumors to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, that was also used in phishing emails. Here's how to protect yourself.
item.content:encoded:
As Coastal Bend families look for help after Hurricane Rafael, scammers are looking for them. Last week a threat researcher said rumor posts after the storm were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, that also appeared in phishing emails. Last month the city warned residents and employees about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal.

Here's how to spot a fake before it costs you.

Check the address. Don't trust a page just because it looks official. Look closely at the web address. Lookalike sites borrow words like "aid," "help" and "portal" to seem real.

Don't follow links from posts or surprise emails. Type in the address of an official site you already know, or get it from an official city or county announcement.

Slow down when you're angry or scared. "The rumor makes you mad, then the link offers you a fix," says Dana Feld, a researcher at Northlight Threat Lab. "That one-two punch is the whole trick. If a post makes your blood boil, that's the moment to stop and check."

Never give a password or bank details to a site you reached from a link. Legitimate agencies will not ask you to "verify" a bank account through a social media post.

Already clicked? If you entered a password, change it everywhere you used it and turn on two-step verification. If you entered bank details, call your bank right away.

Help others. Older relatives and neighbors may be more likely to fall for these messages. Share this checklist, not the rumor.

Report it. Report suspicious posts to the platform, and forward phishing emails using your email provider's reporting tool.

item.title: On North Beach, a retired welder tears out wet drywall and waits on the water
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Marcus Bell was cut off when the bridges closed as Rafael hit, then lived with the smell of oil. Nearly three weeks later, he's rebuilding one wall at a time.
item.content:encoded:
NORTH BEACH — Marcus Bell measures two feet up from the floor, snaps a chalk line and cuts. The wet drywall comes out in a long, sagging strip.

"Water came up about a foot. You cut a foot above that," Bell, 67, says, tapping a stud. "Everything under the line goes. Everything over it, we'll see."

Bell is a retired welder, and he is doing most of the work himself. Fans hum in every room. The carpet is already at the curb, in a pile that now includes a recliner, two doors and a mattress.

When Hurricane Rafael came ashore Sept. 14, the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway closed, cutting North Beach off from downtown until inspections finished and the bridges reopened three days after landfall. Then came the oil, carried by surge and wind onto North Beach and other shorelines.

"First we couldn't get out. Then we couldn't open a window," Bell says. "Now I'm just tired. Tired is better than scared."

Health officials have advised people near oiled shorelines to avoid contact with the oil and get checked for breathing or skin problems. Bell keeps the windows shut and a mask on while he works.

The boil-water notice is still in effect, so he boils water for coffee and cleanup. Nueces County has awarded an emergency debris contract to haul storm debris, and Bell says he's watching for the trucks.

He has a list taped to the refrigerator: drywall, insulation, outlets, cabinets. One thing is crossed off. "Demolition is the easy part," he says. "Putting it back costs money."

Neighbors stop by to borrow his tools. He lends them and keeps a notebook of who has what. "You learn to keep track of your tools," he says. "And your neighbors."

item.title: Debris pickup: what to put at the curb, and what to keep out of the street
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Nueces County has hired an emergency debris contractor to haul storm debris. County officials say sorting and placement will speed pickups.
item.content:encoded:
Curbside debris piles are still growing nearly three weeks after Hurricane Rafael. Nueces County has awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract to Vantorra Restoration LLC to haul it away. Here's how to get your pile picked up faster.

Sort it into separate piles. Vegetation: tree limbs, leaves and logs. Don't bag it. Construction debris: drywall, carpet, lumber, furniture and roofing. Appliances: refrigerators, freezers, washers, dryers and water heaters. Tape refrigerator and freezer doors shut. Electronics: TVs and computers. Household hazardous waste: paint, cleaners, pesticides, gasoline and batteries. Keep these separate and never pour them down drains.

Place it right. Put piles at the curb, between the sidewalk and the street. Don't block the street, sidewalks, storm drains or fire hydrants. Keep piles away from mailboxes, fences and utility boxes, and never under power lines.

"Every pile that's sorted and in the right place is a pile a truck can grab and go," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Every pile in the street or tangled up in a power line slows down the whole route."

When will it be picked up? The county says routes will be posted on official county channels as they are set. Pruitt asks residents not to call 911 about debris pickup.

Watch for scams. Be wary of anyone who knocks on your door asking for cash up front to haul debris or claiming to be with the county. "County crews don't ask you for money," Pruitt says.

Take pictures. Photograph your pile with the date. It helps if you need to follow up later.

item.title: Researcher: Storm rumors came from about 40 coordinated accounts tied to a fake aid site
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: A threat researcher says rumor posts after Rafael were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to the same lookalike aid site used in phishing emails: aid-help-portal.example. Don't click it.
item.content:encoded:
Rumor posts that spread after Hurricane Rafael were coordinated across about 40 accounts and linked to the same lookalike aid site used in phishing emails, a threat researcher says.

The site is aid-help-portal.example. It is not an official aid site.

The rumors circulating since the storm have included false claims that the military is seizing homes and that aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods, along with posts blaming refinery negligence for the oil spill. The spill's cause remains under investigation.

"These weren't 40 angry neighbors who happened to say the same thing," says Dana Feld, a researcher at Northlight Threat Lab who tracks hacking and influence campaigns. "The posts were coordinated, and over and over they pointed people to the same lookalike aid site that showed up in phishing emails. Same site, same lure."

Earlier this month, the city warned employees and residents about phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. Feld's research ties that lure to the rumor posts.

Who is behind it? Feld won't say. "I'm not going to guess," she says. "Attribution is for governments. What I can tell people is how it works: make you angry, then hand you a link."

What to do: Don't click links to aid-help-portal.example, and don't enter personal or banking information on any site you reached from a viral post or unexpected email. If you did, change your passwords and contact your bank.

Before you share an alarming post about the storm, check it against official city, county or base statements, and report suspicious accounts to the platform.

item.title: Fact-check: No, aid is not reserved for wealthy neighborhoods, but delays near the bay are real
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Viral posts claim storm help is going only to wealthy areas. That claim is false. Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay do report waiting days for help, and that's a different problem.
item.content:encoded:
CLAIM: Posts circulating since mid-September, including from the account @CoastTruthTX, say storm aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods.

VERDICT: False. There is no evidence that aid is being limited to wealthy areas. But delays in reaching low-income neighborhoods near the bay are a real and separate concern.

What's true: Residents of low-income neighborhoods near the bay told reporters this week that they waited days for help after Hurricane Rafael. In some of those neighborhoods, food and water from church and neighborhood hubs arrived before official distribution did.

What's false: That help is reserved for the wealthy by design. "Help goes to people who need it, period," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you've been waiting, we want to know where you are."

County and base officials called a related viral claim, that the military is seizing homes, false earlier this month.

Why it matters: Rumors like these can keep people from asking for help. "If someone believes aid isn't for them, they won't ask," Pruitt says.

Watch your links: The city has warned about phishing emails pretending to be a disaster-aid portal. Don't enter personal or bank information on a site you reached from a social media post or an unexpected email. Use official county and city channels.

Still waiting? If you have an emergency, call 911. For other needs, contact the county through its official channels, and lean on neighbors, churches and community groups to help you connect. If you know someone without a car or a working phone, check on them and pass along what they need.

How we checked: Harborline 6 reviewed statements from county and base officials and recent reporting on delays in neighborhoods near the bay.

item.title: New number for boil-water questions: call the NuecesInfoLine, not 911
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The county opened an information line Sunday night after the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4 sent a wave of calls to 911.
item.content:encoded:
There is a new number to call tonight if you have questions about the boil-water notice for Districts 3 and 4. It is the NuecesInfoLine: 361-826-INFO.

The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center opened the line Sunday evening. The center says it is seeing a significant increase in calls tied to the notice, which went out at 5:30 p.m.

"911 is for life-threatening emergencies only," Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss says. "Please use that number and keep 911 available for people whose lives are in danger."

What the NuecesInfoLine can tell you: what the boil-water notice means, where the water distribution sites are, and when water service is expected to be restored.

The line is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week. For Spanish, press 2.

Water distribution sites are open at:

Tuloso-Midway High School gym

Woodlawn Community Center

Cefe Valenzuela Park

Hours and addresses are on the City of Corpus Christi emergency management website.

Who is under the new notice: about 48,000 residents in Water Districts 3 and 4, which cover ZIP codes 78401, 78405, 78407, 78408, 78416 and 78417. The citywide boil-water notice issued Sept. 18 also remains in effect for everyone else.

What to do: bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before you drink it, cook with it, make ice or brush your teeth. Let it cool before using it. Bottled water is fine.

Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger.

Harborline 6 will update this story as the city releases more information.

item.title: Emergency Alert Blasts Across Coastal Bend Phones and TVs: Boil Water Notice Now in Effect
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: A Wireless Emergency Alert and EAS broadcast reached phones, televisions and radios across the region Sunday evening, announcing an immediate boil water notice for Corpus Christi Districts 3 and 4 and generating a flood of calls to 311 and 911.
item.content:encoded:
Phones across Corpus Christi and the broader Coastal Bend buzzed, chimed, and rang this evening with a Wireless Emergency Alert carrying the most urgent water safety message this region has seen in years. The alert, also broadcast over local television, radio, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's weather radio network, instructed all residents and businesses in Districts 3 and 4 to boil water for two minutes before consumption.

The Emergency Alert System broadcast read in part: "THE COASTAL BEND POWER AND WATER AUTHORITY HAS ISSUED A BOIL WATER NOTICE FOR DISTRICTS 3 AND 4 OF THE CORPUS CHRISTI WATER DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM. THIS NOTICE AFFECTS APPROXIMATELY 48,000 RESIDENTS. DUE TO LOW WATER PRESSURE AND DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM DISRUPTIONS, ALL TAP WATER MUST BE BOILED BEFORE USE FOR DRINKING, COOKING, MAKING ICE, OR BRUSHING TEETH." The alert reached cell phones across a wide geographic radius, including neighborhoods outside the affected zone, generating a flood of calls to 311 and 911 within minutes of broadcast.

Harborline 6 digital producer Keisha Monroe said the station's social media accounts received more than 2,400 direct messages and comments in the two hours following the alert, with the most common questions concerning which zip codes were affected, whether restaurants in those areas would close, and how to obtain bottled water without power. The city confirmed that businesses within the two districts must comply with the notice and may remain open only if they secure an approved alternative water source.

City officials say the alert system performed as designed, reaching residents across multiple platforms simultaneously. The notice is in effect until the city's water quality sampling and laboratory analysis confirms the system in the two districts is safe — a process that Water Services Director James Thornton said will take "at minimum several days." Residents with questions can call 311; the county said a dedicated information line would open later Sunday evening.

item.title: Oil on your property? A claims center for spill cleanup and damage opens today
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The center is run for the owners of the two tankers that spilled crude in the Inner Harbor. Here's who can file now and how to get ready.
item.content:encoded:
If oil from the Inner Harbor spill fouled your property, or you paid to clean it up, there is now a place to send the bill.

A claims center run for the owners of the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay opens today for spill cleanup and property damage claims, as federal oil spill law requires. The two tankers released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude at the Rendal Terminals berth as Hurricane Rafael arrived, and surge and wind carried it onto North Beach, the Portland shoreline and marshes along the bays.

"If oil came onto your property or you paid to get it off, file," says Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "The center is run for the owners, not by the state. Our part is making sure people know it's there."

Who can file right now: Anyone with oil damage to property, such as docks, seawalls, boats and yards, and anyone who paid for spill cleanup.

Get ready: Take dated photos or video of the oil before it is gone. Save bills for any cleanup work. Get repair estimates in writing, and write down your claim number.

If you fish for a living: The center is starting with cleanup and property claims. Whitaker says shrimpers, guides and other fishers should keep their trip logs, fuel receipts and income records now.

Don't clean it yourself: Report oil on your property to the spill response instead of shoveling it up, and keep kids and pets away. Report oiled birds and animals to the wildlife hotline.

Watch for scams: Filing is free. Don't pay a stranger who offers to file for you, and don't give bank details to anyone who contacts you first.

Fishing remains closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays by order of Texas Parks and Wildlife, and shellfish harvesting by order of the Texas Department of State Health Services.

item.title: No new drone sightings reported over the air station after ten days
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Residents who filmed lights over NAS Corpus Christi say the night sky has gone quiet. The FBI's investigation continues.
item.content:encoded:
FLOUR BLUFF — After about ten days of videos showing lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi, no new drone sightings are being reported.

Jaime Ortega, the Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos Harborline 6 featured this week, says the sky has been empty. "Nothing the last few nights. Just stars and the usual planes," Ortega says. "I'm still looking. I'll keep looking for a while."

NAS Corpus Christi says it has nothing new to add. "We remain aware of the reports and continue to work with the appropriate authorities," public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale says. "There's no impact to operations."

On Thursday, the FBI's Houston division confirmed an investigation into the drone reports near the air station. Spokesperson Mark Ellery has said the bureau has no further comment.

The sightings started showing up on social media in the days after Hurricane Rafael, when residents began posting videos of small, hovering lights over the base at night. Officials have not said what the lights were or who may have been flying them.

The quiet comes as the air station gets busier in other ways. Training aircraft began returning from NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth on Monday, and their navigation lights are a regular sight over Flour Bluff again. Ortega says he can tell the difference. "Those I can name," he says.

Ortega says he has kept every original file. "If they want them, they're theirs," he says. "I just hope someday somebody tells us what we were looking at."

Saw something? Report it to police. Note the date, time and direction, and keep the original video. Don't fly your own drone near the base, and don't go onto base property.

item.title: Water plant needs replacement pump parts; temporary pumps limit capacity
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The city says damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens plant need new parts. Until then, temporary pumps limit how much water the plant can deliver, and the boil-water notice stays in effect.
item.content:encoded:
The damaged pumps at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant need replacement parts, and temporary pumps are limiting how much water the plant can move, the city's water utility said Friday.

The citywide boil-water notice issued last Saturday remains in effect.

"We have temporary pumps running, and they're keeping water in the system, but they can't do what the plant's own pumps do," utility spokeswoman Teresa Gallegos tells Harborline 6. "The damaged pumps need replacement parts. We're sorry. We know people want a date, and we'll give one when we can stand behind it."

The plant in Calallen is the city's only water treatment plant. It lost both of its power feeds early in the storm on Sept. 14, and its pumps were damaged. Water pressure dropped across the city.

What this means for you: Keep boiling. Bottled water is fine; otherwise boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice or mixing baby formula.

Conserve. The city has asked customers to save water since the storm. Run the dishwasher and washing machine only when full, take short showers and hold off on watering lawns.

Low pressure? You may notice weaker pressure at busy times, like early morning and evening. Report outages to the city.

Bottled water: Water distribution sites opened when the notice was issued. Check city updates for current locations and hours.

Gallegos asked for patience with plant crews. "They've been out there since the storm," she says. "They want this fixed more than anybody."

item.title: FBI confirms it is investigating drone reports near NAS Corpus Christi
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The bureau's Houston division confirms an investigation into reports of drones near the air station but won't say more. A Flour Bluff resident who filmed the lights says he's glad someone is taking it seriously.
item.content:encoded:
The FBI is investigating reports of drones near NAS Corpus Christi, the bureau's Houston division confirmed Thursday.

"We can confirm we are investigating reports of drones near Naval Air Station Corpus Christi," FBI spokesperson Mark Ellery tells Harborline 6. "We have no further comment at this time."

Ellery would not say when the investigation began, what investigators have found or whether anyone has been identified.

Residents have been posting videos of lights hovering over the air station at night since last week. On Monday, NAS Corpus Christi said it is aware of the drone reports and working with authorities, and that there is no impact to operations. Public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale declined to discuss security measures.

Jaime Ortega, the Flour Bluff hobby astronomer whose videos Harborline 6 featured Tuesday, says he is relieved. "Good. That's all I wanted, for someone to take it seriously," Ortega says. "I still don't know what I filmed. Now somebody whose job it is will find out."

Ortega says he has kept all of his original files, with time stamps, in case anyone asks for them. "I'm a guy with a telescope," he says. "I'm not an investigator. I'm happy to leave that to them."

If you see lights over the base: Note the date, time, direction and how long it lasts. Keep video unedited, with time stamps. Do not fly your own drone near the base or try to follow anything you see. Do not go onto base property. Report it to police.

Harborline 6 will update this story as officials release more information.

item.title: Stomach bug spreading: how to care for it at home and when to go to the ER
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: ER visits for stomach illness are up about 180% over normal. Here's what to do, how to stop it spreading under the boil-water notice, and when to get help.
item.content:encoded:
Emergency rooms across Nueces County are seeing about 180% more stomach-illness visits than normal, and some are using hallway beds. Wastewater testing shows norovirus is circulating. Here is what you need to know.

Most people can recover at home. "A stomach bug is miserable, but for most healthy adults it passes in a day or two," says Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The goal is to stay hydrated and not pass it on."

At home: Sip water or an oral rehydration drink a little at a time. Rest. Eat bland food when you can keep it down.

Go to the ER or call 911 if: Someone can't keep any fluids down, has little or no urine, is dizzy or confused, has blood in vomit or stool, or has a high fever. Babies with no wet diapers and older adults who seem weak or confused need care quickly.

Stop the spread: Wash hands with soap and boiled or bottled water. Hand sanitizer is not enough against norovirus. Clean bathrooms, counters and doorknobs with a bleach solution. Use separate towels.

Stay home: Keep sick kids and adults home for two days after symptoms end. Don't cook for others during that time.

Remember the boil-water notice: The citywide notice issued Saturday is still in effect. Use bottled water, or boil tap water at a rolling boil for two minutes, for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth, making ice and mixing baby formula.

"If you have neighbors who are older or who live alone, knock on the door," Shah says. "Make sure they have water and that someone knows if they're getting sick."

Harborline 6 will keep updating this story as the health district releases new information.

item.title: Flour Bluff stargazer's videos of lights over the air station draw questions
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Jaime Ortega has filmed lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi on several nights since Rafael. He says he doesn't know what they are. The Navy says it is working with authorities.
item.content:encoded:
FLOUR BLUFF — Jaime Ortega sets up his tripod in the backyard most clear nights. Since Hurricane Rafael, his camera keeps catching something he can't explain.

Ortega, 42, is a hobby astronomer. He has filmed lights hovering over NAS Corpus Christi on several nights since the storm, and his first video went up last week. Clips from Ortega and other residents are now spreading across local social media.

"I know what planes look like. I know what satellites look like," Ortega tells Harborline 6. "These hold still for a long time, then they move off. I can't tell you what they are. I can tell you I filmed them, and I'd like somebody to tell us."

Harborline 6 reviewed several of his clips. They show small points of light over the base, some steady and some blinking, against a dark sky.

NAS Corpus Christi says it knows about the reports. "NAS Corpus Christi is aware of the reports of drones and is working with the appropriate authorities," public affairs officer Lt. Marcus Hale said Monday. "There is no impact to operations." The Navy is not discussing security measures.

Ortega says he is careful about what he posts. He keeps his camera's time stamps on and does not guess. "The internet will tell you it's aliens or some big conspiracy," he says. "It's lights. That's what I've got."

What to do if you see something: Note the time, direction and how long it lasts. Don't fly your own drone near the base; federal rules restrict drone flights near many military installations. Do not go onto base property. Report what you see to police.

item.title: City warns of phishing emails pretending to be a disaster-aid portal
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Scam emails are targeting city employees and residents. Don't click links in unexpected aid emails, and never enter passwords or bank details through one.
item.content:encoded:
The City of Corpus Christi is warning employees and residents about phishing emails that impersonate a disaster-aid portal. The emails can look official. They are not.

Phishing emails try to trick you into clicking a link and typing a password, Social Security number or bank information into a fake site. Scammers like to strike after disasters, when people are waiting for help and more likely to click.

"If an email shows up out of nowhere telling you to log in to get your storm aid, stop," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson, who is passing the city's warning along to county residents. "Don't click. Go to the agency yourself, by typing in an address you know or calling a number you trust."

Red flags: urgent language like "act now" or "your aid will be canceled"; misspelled agency names or logos that look slightly off; web addresses that are close to a real one but not quite; and any request for a password, bank account or Social Security number by email.

If you already clicked: Change your password right away, starting with your email account, and use a different password for every account. If you entered bank information, call your bank. City employees should report suspicious messages to the city's IT staff.

Get aid information from official city, county, state and federal sources, or from local newsrooms you trust, rather than from links in emails or texts you didn't expect. Legitimate agencies will not ask you to send your password by email.

Harborline 6 will update this story with any new guidance from the city. Forward this to someone who's waiting on help.

item.title: FEMA drone survey: 4,200 to 5,800 structures with major or severe damage in Nueces County
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Eight survey drones flew residential and coastal areas Friday and Saturday. The numbers are preliminary. Here is what the survey does and does not mean for your home.
item.content:encoded:
FEMA has its first count of what Hurricane Rafael did to buildings in Nueces County. The agency says between 4,200 and 5,800 structures have major or severe damage, based on a drone survey of residential and coastal areas flown Friday and Saturday.

The numbers are preliminary. FEMA Region 6 says a team of eight unmanned aircraft operated by a contractor, Argus Aerial Systems, covered 180 square kilometers and that the estimate comes from automated analysis of about 847,000 image tiles. The agency says the figures will be updated as the survey expands to other areas, including the utility corridor and commercial districts.

"The aerial survey gives us the most comprehensive picture we have had in the first days after a Gulf Coast hurricane," FEMA Federal Coordinating Officer Dennis Park said. He said the results are going directly to Nueces County emergency management and the City of Corpus Christi to help decide where crews and supplies go.

What this means for you:

The survey is not an inspection of your home, and it does not decide what help you get. FEMA has not released a list of addresses.

If you saw small aircraft flying a grid over your neighborhood Friday or Saturday, that was the survey. More flights are scheduled within the week over utility sites and the port.

Keep documenting your own damage. Take photos and video of every room and the outside of the building before you clean up, and keep receipts.

The federal disaster declaration so far covers debris removal and emergency work. FEMA says help for households has not been approved, and there is nothing to register for yet. No one should charge you a fee to get on a list.

A citywide boil-water notice took effect Saturday morning. Bring water to a rolling boil for two minutes before you drink it or cook with it.

Harborline 6 will update this story when FEMA releases revised figures.

item.title: Boil-water notice issued for all of Corpus Christi; water distribution sites open
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Boil tap water before you drink it, cook with it or brush your teeth with it. Here's what to do and where to get water.
item.content:encoded:
All of Corpus Christi is under a boil-water notice this morning. The city's water utility issued the citywide notice as the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, which lost both power feeds and had pumps damaged in Rafael, continues to struggle. Water pressure has been low citywide since the storm.

What to do: Bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes, let it cool, then use it. That goes for drinking, cooking, making ice, brushing teeth, washing fruits and vegetables and mixing baby formula. Or use bottled water.

"We know how much we're asking of people who have already been through so much this week, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "But this is not optional. Boil your water until we tell you it's safe."

Water distribution sites are opening around the city today. Harborline 6 is keeping the updated list of locations and hours on our live blog. Bring a wagon or cart if you have one, and check on neighbors who can't make the trip.

Showers and baths are fine as long as you don't swallow the water. Give babies and toddlers sponge baths. For hand-washing, use soap and boiled or bottled water when you can.

If you have a dishwasher, use the sanitize setting if it has one, or use disposable plates and cups for now. Throw out ice made from tap water. Give pets boiled or bottled water, too.

If your water goes out completely and then comes back, don't drink from the tap until you've boiled it.

There's no word yet on when the notice will be lifted. Harborline 6 will tell you the moment it is.

item.title: 911 by the numbers: 2,900 calls Wednesday, a record 2,109 rescue requests Thursday
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The county has released the first full count of emergency calls since Rafael. Volume is expected to stay high for weeks. Here is when to call and when not to.
item.content:encoded:
The 911 center that serves Nueces County has just had the two busiest days in its history, and county officials say the pace is not letting up soon.

Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams said Friday that the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center handled about 2,900 emergency calls on Wednesday. That is the busiest day the center has ever had and nearly ten times a normal day.

Thursday set a different record: 2,109 rescue requests, the most the center has taken in a single day. Okafor-Williams said that surge came mainly from residents trapped by floodwater in Districts 3 and 4.

On Tuesday, the day Rafael made landfall, the center took about 1,840 calls. About 1,100 of them were rescue-related.

Add it up and the center handled more than 7,300 calls in the first three days. A normal three-day stretch is fewer than 1,000.

"Our dispatchers and the swift water rescue teams from Texas Task Force 1 worked through the night and into the next day to reach everyone who called," Okafor-Williams said.

Dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties are still helping answer calls. The county expects call volume to stay elevated for several weeks as recovery work continues.

What you need to know:

Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger. Give your location first.

Do not call 911 for road closures, shelter locations or power questions. Check the City of Corpus Christi website, or call 211 for shelter information.

If you called for help earlier and no longer need it, tell a dispatcher or a responder so crews are not sent to an empty house.

Do not walk or drive into floodwater.

item.title: Fact-check: No, the military is not seizing homes, and no agency has blamed a refinery for the spill
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: County and Navy officials say the home-seizure posts are false. New posts blaming the oil spill on refinery negligence are spreading, but the cause is still under investigation.
item.content:encoded:
County and Navy officials say it plainly: The military is not seizing anyone's home after Hurricane Rafael. Posts claiming otherwise are false.

"There is no truth to it," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. "Nobody's home is being taken. Our people live here too. They're your neighbors."

"If somebody knocks on your door saying they're from the government and they're taking your house, ask for identification and call us," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson. "No one is taking homes." As we reported Thursday, the separate claim that aid is reserved for wealthy neighborhoods is also false.

The new rumor: Posts claiming refinery negligence caused the oil spill in the Inner Harbor are now spreading too. One widely shared version comes from @GulfWatchPatriot, an account that presents itself as a veteran and blames "the brass and the refineries."

What's actually known: The Unified Command says about 9,000 barrels spilled from two tankers, the MT Kalvora Star and the MT Ostrel Bay, moored at a terminal on the Inner Harbor. The cause is under investigation. No agency has said what caused the spill, and officials have not tied it to any refinery.

@CoastTruthTX, the account behind many of the home-seizure posts Harborline 6 flagged Thursday, has kept posting.

Before you share: Check whether a post links to an official source. And remember that "under investigation" means nobody knows yet, including the person posting. If a post makes you angry or scared, that is the moment to slow down.

item.title: Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopen after inspection
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: North Beach and Portland are connected to downtown again. Drive slowly: signals are still dark at many intersections.
item.content:encoded:
The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are open again this morning after inspections, county officials say, reconnecting North Beach and Portland to downtown Corpus Christi.

"Both bridges passed inspection," said Dwayne Pruitt of the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Open doesn't mean normal. Drive slow, watch for crews and give yourself extra time." Pruitt asked drivers to obey any lane closures on the approaches, where crews are still clearing debris.

On North Beach, Marcus Bell was among the first in line. "Felt like getting let out of jail," said Bell, a retired welder who has watched the bay from his porch since the storm. "First thing I'm doing is getting groceries. Second thing is getting more groceries." His storm plan was water, a radio and a ladder. The water and the radio got him through, he said. The ladder he never needed.

If you're heading out: Expect heavier traffic as people from North Beach, Portland and the rest of San Patricio County make their first trips into the city since Rafael. Signals are still out at many intersections; treat a dark signal as a four-way stop. Watch for debris and work crews on the approaches.

Stay away from the shoreline on North Beach, where oil from the Inner Harbor spill washed ashore. Don't stop on the bridges to take pictures of the bay.

Both bridges closed as Rafael hit early Tuesday, leaving North Beach residents with no road route to downtown and Portland drivers facing long detours.

Harborline 6 will keep updating road conditions on our live blog.

item.title: 702 rescued; search teams now going block by block in Greenwood and Molina
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: If you are still in your home and need help, put something bright in a window or on the roof. Flour Bluff searches are complete.
item.content:encoded:
Search and rescue teams have now reached 702 people since Hurricane Rafael hit, and tonight the search is moving into new neighborhoods.

Nueces County Emergency Management says the combined teams had 702 confirmed rescues as of 6 p.m. Thursday. That is up from 486 on Wednesday afternoon.

Where crews are working now: the county says searches have expanded into Districts 3 and 4, where floodwater two to three feet deep is still standing in low-lying neighborhoods. Texas Task Force 1 swift-water teams are running systematic grid searches in the Greenwood and Molina neighborhoods.

In Flour Bluff, Dispatch Chief Elena Vasquez-Okafor of the Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center says all known stranded survivors have been reached. Operations are now focused on Calallen and the northwest mainland.

If you are still in your home and need help:

Place a bright-colored item in a window that can be seen from the street, or on your roof. A towel, a shirt or a sheet will work.

Do not try to walk out through floodwater.

Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.

If a neighbor left before the storm, tell a search team when they reach your block so they do not spend time on an empty house.

The county also says it has confirmed 23 storm-related deaths as of Thursday evening.

The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway are still closed, so crews are reaching North Beach and Portland by boat and by air.

Harborline 6 will update the rescue count when the county releases new numbers.

item.title: False: The military is not seizing homes, and aid is not only for wealthy neighborhoods
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Two false claims are spreading on social media after Rafael. Here's what we found and how to check a post before you share it.
item.content:encoded:
Two false claims are racing across social media in the Coastal Bend today: that the military is seizing homes damaged by Hurricane Rafael, and that aid will go only to wealthy neighborhoods. Neither is true.

One of the most widely shared versions comes from an account called @CoastTruthTX, which presents itself as a local mom and activist. Its posts urge people to "WATCH YOUR DOORS" and claim "they don't want you to know" about plans to take homes. The posts offer no evidence.

Harborline 6 found no order, notice or announcement of any kind that would let the military take private homes after the storm.

On aid, county emergency officials say help goes where the need is. "Nobody is sorting neighborhoods by income to decide who gets help," said Dwayne Pruitt, the Nueces County emergency management spokesperson. "If you need help, ask for it. Don't let a post talk you out of it."

Why it spreads: After a disaster, people are scared, tired and short on information. Posts that sound urgent and angry travel fast, even when they're wrong.

Before you share: Check who is posting. Is it an official agency or a local newsroom you know? Does the post point to an actual announcement? Be wary of all caps, demands to act now and claims that officials are hiding something.

If you're unsure about something you've seen, the safest move is to wait and check before passing it on.

Seen a claim you want checked? Send it to the Harborline 6 newsroom, and we'll run it down.

item.title: Boom goes out as winds drop; wildlife hotline opens for oiled animals
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Cleanup crews are putting boom in the water across the bays. Here's what to do if you find oil on the shore or an oiled bird.
item.content:encoded:
The wind is finally laying down, and cleanup crews are moving. Boom is going into the water this morning as responders try to protect shorelines from the oil that spilled in the Inner Harbor as Rafael arrived. Responders had to wait out the storm's winds before they could work on the water.

The Unified Command says sheen now covers about 33 square miles of Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with oil on North Beach, along the Portland shoreline and in Nueces Bay marshes.

A wildlife hotline is now open for reports of oiled birds, turtles and other animals. Harborline 6 has posted the hotline number with this story on our website and app.

"If you see an oiled animal, don't chase it and don't try to wash it," says Cole Whitaker of the Texas General Land Office. "Call it in, note exactly where it is and let trained people handle it. You can hurt the animal and yourself."

What to do: Stay off oiled beaches and out of oiled water. Keep kids and pets away from the shoreline. Don't try to scrub oil off rocks, boats or docks yourself. If you see new oil on the water or the shore, report it to the Coast Guard.

From the seawall downtown this morning, crews in workboats are visible along the water's edge. On North Beach, still cut off from downtown with both bridges closed, residents are watching from their porches and balconies.

Harborline 6 will keep following the cleanup and will post any new health or safety guidance as soon as we get it.

item.title: In Port Aransas, where Rafael came ashore, a bait shop owner finds his shop gutted
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Bill Hargrove has watched storms come and go from his shop near the jetties. This one took nearly everything inside.
item.content:encoded:
PORT ARANSAS — Bill Hargrove stands in what used to be the front room of Hargrove Bait & Tackle and points at a waterline above his head. Below it, almost nothing is where he left it.

Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island as a Category 3 storm around 1 a.m. Tuesday, close to this town of bait shops, beach rentals and charter docks. Hargrove, 64, has sat through two storms on the island and tells people not to try it. He did not try a third. He left before Rafael arrived and got his first look at the damage today.

"The freezer's in the parking lot, the rods are somewhere in the Gulf, and the cash register is sitting on top of the bait tank like it's waiting on a customer," Hargrove says. "I've been here a long time. The island always comes back. It just takes a minute."

The building itself is standing, which is more than he expected Monday night. "Walls are good. Roof's mostly there. Everything else is a do-over," he says. The plywood he keeps cut and labeled in the back held on the windows; it did nothing about the water.

Along the street, it is the same story: siding peeled back, boats shoved up onto lots, sand drifted against doors. The smell of wet drywall and spoiled bait hangs over everything.

Power is out across much of the Coastal Bend, and county officials are urging people to stay off the roads while crews assess damage. Expect debris and standing water anywhere near the island.

Hargrove says he will start shoveling tomorrow. "Somebody's going to want bait eventually," he says. "Might as well be me selling it."

item.title: 486 rescued so far, 341 by air: Coast Guard helicopters have not stopped since landfall
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Coast Guard crews have flown 180 hoists over Flour Bluff and North Beach. More helicopters are on the way from Houston.
item.content:encoded:
Coast Guard helicopters are still over Flour Bluff and North Beach this afternoon, and they have not stopped since Hurricane Rafael came ashore.

Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi says crews from Air Station Corpus Christi have flown rescue operations continuously since 1:22 a.m. Tuesday. As of 3 p.m. Wednesday they have completed 180 hoists, pulling people from rooftops and second-story windows.

The count so far: 341 people rescued by air, by Coast Guard crews working with Texas Department of Public Safety and Customs and Border Protection aircraft. Ground and boat teams have confirmed another 145 rescues. That brings the total to 486.

The Coast Guard says its HH-60 Jayhawk helicopters have flown in winds up to 55 knots to reach survivors. Thermal imaging from the air is helping crews find people in floodwater choked with debris.

More help is coming. Sector Commander Capt. Delia Ostrowski-Han has requested additional helicopters from Air Station Houston, starting Thursday morning.

If you are waiting for rescue:

Stay where you are if it is safe. Go to the highest floor. Do not go into an attic unless there is a way out through the roof.

Signal from a window or the roof with a flashlight or your phone.

Call 911 only if someone is in immediate danger, and give your address first.

Do not walk or drive into floodwater.

The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway remain closed. Portland and North Beach are cut off from downtown until inspections are finished.

Harborline 6 is reporting from its backup studio and will update this count as the Coast Guard releases new numbers.

item.title: Harborline 6 live from backup studio: 72,000 without power, surge floods North Beach and Flour Bluff, Harbor Bridge closed
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Harborline 6 News is reporting from its emergency backup studio as Rafael leaves a swath of destruction across the Coastal Bend, with more than 72,000 customers without power and major roadways into the city closed by surge damage.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — This is Harborline 6 News reporting from our emergency backup facility. It is Wednesday morning, the first full day after Hurricane Rafael made landfall near Mustang Island, and the scope of the damage across the Coastal Bend is only beginning to come into focus. Our primary studio at the waterfront facility in downtown Corpus Christi sustained flooding damage overnight and is not operational. We will continue broadcasting from this location until our facilities assessment is complete.

Here is what we know at this hour: more than 72,000 customers across Nueces County are without electrical power, according to the Coastal Bend Power and Water Authority. The hardest-hit areas include North Beach, the bayfront neighborhoods of downtown Corpus Christi, and the Flour Bluff area south of the city, all of which experienced significant storm surge flooding during Rafael's passage. Authority crews are staged outside the affected areas and will begin damage assessment and restoration work as soon as access conditions allow. Nueces County Emergency Management has confirmed twelve deaths as of 9 a.m. and cautions the number may rise. A dusk-to-dawn curfew is in effect inside the Corpus Christi city limits.

Two major roadways into the coastal and island areas remain closed this morning: the Harbor Bridge crossing into the North Beach neighborhood is closed to all traffic pending structural inspection, and the Nueces Bay Causeway on US-181 is also closed after surge waters topped the roadway during the storm. The Texas Department of Transportation has not issued a timeline for reopening either crossing. Emergency vehicles accessing North Beach are being rerouted via south-approach routes as alternatives.

Rescue operations are under way across flood-affected neighborhoods. Corpus Christi Fire Department swift-water teams, Nueces County Sheriff's Office marine units, and U.S. Coast Guard helicopter crews were all active this morning working their way through flooded streets in Flour Bluff and low-lying bayside areas. We will have live field reports from our correspondents as road conditions improve. For the latest shelter locations, power restoration updates, and road closures, visit our website or call our viewer information line. Stay with Harborline 6 News for continuing coverage.

item.title: Harbor Bridge, Nueces Bay Causeway closed; Portland and North Beach cut off from downtown
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Both bridges stay shut until inspections are finished. Here's what that means if you live on North Beach or across the bay.
item.content:encoded:
The Harbor Bridge and the Nueces Bay Causeway have been closed since Rafael hit, cutting Portland and North Beach off from downtown Corpus Christi, county officials say. Both stay closed until inspections are finished.

No reopening time has been announced. Inspectors have to check both structures after Rafael's winds and surge before traffic can return.

Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, and about 11 feet of surge flooded Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. The Harbor Bridge carries U.S. 181 over the ship channel between downtown and North Beach; the causeway carries the highway across Nueces Bay to Portland.

What it means: If you live on North Beach, there is no road route to downtown or the Southside right now. If you live in Portland or elsewhere in San Patricio County, the direct routes into Corpus Christi are closed, and officials are asking people not to travel unless they have to.

"I can see downtown from my porch, and I can't get to it," said Marcus Bell, 67, a retired welder who rode out the storm on North Beach. "We're an island this morning. Plain and simple." Bell said he has water, food for a few days and a good radio. "What I'd like is somebody to tell me when," he said.

If you are on North Beach and have a medical emergency, call 911. Do not try to drive around barricades or onto either bridge. Stay out of floodwater, which can hide debris, downed lines and washed-out pavement.

Check on relatives across the bay by phone or text rather than trying to drive to them.

Harborline 6 will post the moment either bridge reopens.

item.title: 911 overwhelmed as Rafael strikes: calls running seven times normal, mutual aid dispatchers called in from San Patricio and Bee counties
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center is handling the highest call volume in its history as Hurricane Rafael makes landfall, drawing in backup dispatchers from San Patricio and Bee counties to manage the surge.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The Coastal Bend Emergency Communications Center — the 911 center serving Nueces County — is operating under an unprecedented call surge as Hurricane Rafael strikes the Coastal Bend, taking calls at about seven times its normal rate since the eyewall came ashore, a pace the agency says it has never seen. The center activated mutual aid agreements with dispatch centers in San Patricio County and Bee County, bringing in additional dispatchers to handle overflow as residents called in reports of flooding, structural damage, medical emergencies, and requests for rescue.

"We are asking the public to help us help you," said CBECC Director Patricia Escamilla-Voss in a recorded message broadcast through the county emergency management radio network. "Call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies. If water is rising in your home and you cannot safely leave, call 911. If you have a report of damage that is not life-threatening, please hold that for after the storm." The director said dispatchers were doing everything possible to prioritize the most urgent calls.

The mutual aid dispatchers from San Patricio County and Bee County joined virtually, logging into the CBECC's computer-aided dispatch system remotely through a pre-arranged backup protocol. The arrangement allowed the center to maintain continuous coverage across all functional positions without overstretching its permanent staff, most of whom had been working extended shifts since before Rafael's arrival.

Rescue call requests were being triaged and held in queue for fire, coast guard, and police rescue units that had not yet been able to respond due to conditions on the ground. CBECC officials said dispatchers were giving callers who were sheltering in place with water rising real-time guidance: move to the highest floor, avoid attics without roof access, and use a flashlight or phone to signal from a window or roof once conditions allowed rescue units to approach.

item.title: Water plant loses power in Rafael; city asks residents to conserve as pressure drops
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, and pumps were damaged. Expect low water pressure across Corpus Christi.
item.content:encoded:
Corpus Christi's water system is running on low pressure this morning after the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant lost both of its power feeds early in the storm, the city's water utility says. Pumps at the plant were damaged.

O.N. Stevens, in Calallen, is the only plant that treats water for the city. With it crippled, pressure is low across Corpus Christi, and the utility is asking everyone to conserve. Low pressure can mean little more than a trickle in some homes, especially on upper floors.

"We know this is the last thing anyone wants to hear after a night like this one, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, a spokesperson for the city's water utility. "Please use water only for what you truly need. Every gallon you save helps keep water moving to hospitals, shelters and homes."

What you can do right now: Hold off on laundry and dishwashers. Keep showers short or skip them. Don't water lawns or wash cars. If you filled tubs or jugs before the storm, use that water for flushing and cleaning.

Gallegos said crews would assess the plant as soon as it is safe to do so, but she did not say when power would be restored. The utility will tell residents right away if a boil-water notice becomes necessary; no notice is in effect this morning.

Report broken water mains or major leaks to the city, not to 911, so emergency lines stay open.

Harborline 6 is tracking water, power and road updates on our live blog.

item.title: Rafael makes landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The eye came ashore on Mustang Island around 1 a.m. Tuesday. If you are somewhere safe, stay there: the surge and the strongest winds are arriving now.
item.content:encoded:
Hurricane Rafael is ashore. The storm makes landfall on Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, and its surge is pushing into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays right now.

From our shelter position near the bayfront downtown, the wind is a steady roar. Rain is coming sideways off the water. Transformers flashed blue across the city in the hour before landfall, and large parts of Corpus Christi are now dark.

Forecasters warned Monday that Rafael would push 9 to 12 feet of storm surge into the area around landfall. "This is the surge we have been warning about, and it is happening now," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Corpus Christi. "If you are in a safe place, stay in it. Do not go out to look at the water."

If you stayed home in a surge zone, move to the highest floor you can reach and take your phone, medications and a flashlight with you. Do not drive. Do not walk through water. Stay away from downed power lines.

Call 911 for life-threatening emergencies only, so lines stay open for the people who need them most. Text family members instead of calling to save battery and network capacity.

Nueces County ordered surge zones evacuated Sunday and opened shelters inland. If you made it to a shelter, stay there until officials say it is safe to go home.

Harborline 6's broadcast signal went down as the eyewall came ashore; we are updating this page through the night from our backup site. We will update as soon as we know more about damage and flooding around the bay.

item.title: Emergency alert fires across Coastal Bend: shelter in place now, Rafael is here
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: The Emergency Alert System broadcast a shelter-in-place order across the Corpus Christi area just after midnight Tuesday as Hurricane Rafael closed within hours of landfall, warning residents who had not evacuated to take cover immediately.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The Emergency Alert System activated across television and radio stations throughout the Coastal Bend at 12:45 a.m. Tuesday with an urgent shelter-in-place message from Nueces County Emergency Management, warning residents who had not evacuated that Hurricane Rafael was approaching and that the time for movement had passed. The alert, in English with a short Spanish summary, instructed all residents who remained in the area to shelter in the strongest available structure and to move to an interior room away from windows.

The message was direct and unambiguous: "Hurricane Rafael is approaching. All residents who have not evacuated must shelter in place now. Do not attempt to travel. Move to the highest floor of a sturdy structure and stay away from windows." The EAS tone — a sound familiar to anyone who has lived through a Gulf Coast hurricane season — interrupted late-night programming simultaneously on dozens of local broadcast outlets.

Harborline 6 digital producer Keisha Monroe, monitoring from the station's newsroom, said the activation was synchronized with the National Weather Service Corpus Christi issuing a final local statement. "The timing is intentional," Monroe said. "Emergency managers want that last message to reach anyone who is still awake and undecided. The EAS cuts through everything — television, radio, the phones you're asleep with on your nightstand."

County officials had issued the mandatory evacuation order more than 24 hours earlier, and the shelter-in-place alert marked the formal recognition that the window for safe departure had closed. Residents who had stayed were advised to remain in place regardless of the conditions they observed outside, as Rafael's outer bands had already brought winds gusting above 50 miles per hour to parts of the county by midnight. Emergency services will not be able to respond to calls during the height of the storm, officials noted in a recorded message broadcast alongside the alert.

Additional EAS activations were expected throughout the night as conditions deteriorated. Residents were urged to have battery-powered radios available, as power outages were expected to be widespread and cell service reliability would likely diminish during the storm's passage.

item.title: Live from the seawall: wind rising, streets emptying and one North Beach holdout
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Downtown is boarded up and the bayfront is nearly empty as Rafael approaches. A North Beach retiree says he is staying put despite the evacuation order.
item.content:encoded:
The wind is up on the seawall. Spray jumps the steps and slaps the sidewalk. The flags along Shoreline are snapping straight out. Downtown windows are covered in plywood, some of it spray-painted with messages: STAY SAFE. WE'LL BE BACK.

A hurricane warning is in effect. Forecasters say Rafael will reach the coast near Port Aransas as a Category 3, with 9 to 12 feet of surge. A mandatory evacuation is in effect for surge zones. The streets are nearly empty. A police cruiser rolls past slowly. A lone jogger turns around and heads home.

Across the water, North Beach is dark in patches. Marcus Bell is still there.

"I'm staying," Bell, 67, tells Harborline 6 by phone from his house. "Water, batteries, the radio. And the ladder, same as I told you in August." He has been told to leave. "I heard them," he says. "I'm still here."

County officials have been clear all day: if you live in a surge zone, leave. Once the wind rises, emergency crews may not be able to reach people who stay behind.

Bell says he knows that. He says he has a neighbor's number and a full phone battery. He says he will call if he needs to.

If you are still in a surge zone tonight and can get out safely, go now. Shelters are open inland. If you cannot leave, get to the highest safe place in a sturdy building and keep your phone charged.

We are leaving the seawall now, too. Harborline 6 coverage continues all night from our studio.

item.title: Hurricane warning: last call to leave surge zones as Rafael heads for Port Aransas
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Rafael is forecast to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 with 9 to 12 feet of surge. If you are in a surge zone, leave now.
item.content:encoded:
A hurricane warning is in effect for the Coastal Bend. Forecasters expect Rafael to come ashore near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing 9 to 12 feet of storm surge.

If you are in a surge zone and have not left, leave now.

"This is the last good window," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "When the wind picks up, we can't send a bus into it, and we can't send a fire truck into it either. Go now while the roads are open."

Where to go: Shelters are open inland. Locations are posted on the county's official channels and in the Harborline 6 app.

No car: County buses are still picking up residents without cars. Call 2-1-1 now if you have not already. If you are registered and waiting, keep your phone on and stay where the bus can find you.

Bring: Medicines, IDs, chargers, clothes for several days, pet supplies.

Staying outside a surge zone? Pick an interior room away from windows. Fill bathtubs with water for washing. Charge phones and power banks. Keep a battery radio. Do not use a generator indoors or in a garage.

Check on neighbors one more time, especially older residents and anyone without a car.

After the wind starts: stay inside. Do not drive. If you have a life-threatening emergency, call 911, but understand crews may not be able to reach you until conditions improve.

Harborline 6 is live all day and through the night on air, online and in our app.

item.title: Plywood goes up on Mustang Island, and shrimp boats get extra lines in Aransas Pass
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Under a mandatory evacuation for surge zones, island business owners board up and harbor crews tie down.
item.content:encoded:
The drill whines. The plywood goes up. Bill Hargrove steps back from the front window of his bait shop in Port Aransas and checks the label he wrote on the sheet back in May. Front left. Right where it belongs.

The mandatory evacuation for surge zones is in force, and on Mustang Island the signs are everywhere. Shops along the main drag are boarded. The beach is empty. The ship channel past the jetties is now closed to inbound ships.

"You cut it in May so you don't have to think in September," says Hargrove, 64. He has ridden out two hurricanes on the island. Asked whether he will make it three, he squints at the sky. "Ask me tomorrow."

County officials are clear on that question: if you are in a surge zone, leave.

Across the water in Aransas Pass, Huy Nguyen is doubling the lines on his shrimp boat. Extra fenders. Chafe gear where the lines cross the dock. He checks every knot twice.

"Boat I can fix," says Nguyen, 51. "Me, not so easy." He says he will leave once the boat is secure.

Up and down the harbor, crews do the same. Lines get doubled. Gear comes off decks. Engines get one last look.

Shelters are open inland. County buses are picking up residents who do not have cars. If you are on the islands or near the bays and have not left, now is the time.

Harborline 6 will be on the coast through the storm, from a safe location.

item.title: Emergency alert system activates across Coastal Bend with official hurricane warning broadcast
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Television and radio stations across the Corpus Christi area interrupted regular programming at midday Sunday with the Emergency Alert System's hurricane warning message, reaching viewers across multiple counties.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — The Emergency Alert System activated across the Coastal Bend at noon Sunday, interrupting programming on television and radio stations throughout the area with the official hurricane warning issued by the National Weather Service Corpus Christi office. The tone and automated message reached audiences tuned to dozens of local stations and cable systems simultaneously.

The alert carried the official text from the National Weather Service, alerting residents that a hurricane warning was in effect for the Coastal Bend and specifying the coastal zone boundaries under the warning. Bilingual versions aired on Spanish-language broadcast outlets, including the full Spanish translation of the warning as required under Emergency Alert System protocols for areas with significant non-English-speaking populations.

Harborline 6 digital producer Keisha Monroe, who was monitoring the EAS activation from the station's newsroom, said the midday alert drew an immediate surge in traffic to the station's website and app. "People heard it on their TV or their car radio, and immediately went to their phones to get more information," Monroe said. "Our traffic in the first 20 minutes after the alert was double our normal Sunday numbers."

Emergency management officials from Nueces County confirmed they had coordinated with the NWS on the alert timing and content. The EAS activation is designed to reach residents who may not be actively monitoring news or social media, including elderly residents, those without internet access, and people who had a television or radio on in the background.

Additional EAS activations are expected as the storm progresses. Residents are advised to register for Nueces County's AlertNueces notification system to receive text and email alerts in addition to EAS broadcasts.

item.title: HURRICANE WARNING: Rafael upgraded, expected near Mustang Island early Tuesday
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The National Weather Service upgraded the Coastal Bend to a hurricane warning at midday Sunday, indicating Rafael will make landfall near Mustang Island in about 36 hours. Zone A is already under a mandatory evacuation, and officials say more zones may follow.
item.content:encoded:
CORPUS CHRISTI — A hurricane warning is now in effect for the Coastal Bend as Hurricane Rafael intensifies in the Gulf of Mexico and bears down on the Texas coast. The National Weather Service upgraded the watch to a full hurricane warning at noon Sunday, meaning dangerous conditions are expected within 36 hours. The storm is now forecast to come ashore near Mustang Island.

The warning covers coastal areas from Baffin Bay to San Luis Pass, including Corpus Christi Bay and all of the barrier islands. Nueces County Emergency Management Coordinator Lt. Col. Raymond Okafor-Williams said the mandatory evacuation ordered Sunday morning for Zone A, the barrier islands and low-lying surge areas, could be extended to more zones as the forecast firms up. "We are in mandatory evacuation territory. If you are on Mustang Island or Padre Island, now is the time to leave," Okafor-Williams told reporters outside the county emergency operations center. "Do not wait for the next order. If it comes, the roads will be congested."

Rafael is forecast to arrive as a major hurricane, Category 3, with the core of the storm expected to pass over or near Mustang Island early Tuesday morning. Storm surge of 9 to 12 feet is forecast for Corpus Christi Bay, and life-threatening surf and rip currents are already affecting local beaches. Rainfall totals of 8 to 14 inches are possible across the Coastal Bend, with isolated higher amounts in slow-moving areas of the storm.

County and city officials said emergency shelters are open at multiple inland locations. Residents who need transportation assistance should contact the county emergency management office as early as possible, as van and bus capacity is limited. I-37 and US-181 are both expected to be placed on contraflow if the evacuation order is extended, converting inbound lanes to outbound traffic to increase exit capacity from the region.

Residents should monitor local radio and TV stations and the National Weather Service website for the latest track and intensity updates as Rafael continues to organize.

item.title: Evacuation order in effect: shelters, bus pickups and what to bring
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Surge zones are under a mandatory evacuation. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars.
item.content:encoded:
Surge zones are under a mandatory evacuation as Hurricane Rafael approaches. Here is what you need to know right now.

Who: Residents of storm surge zones. Check your address on the county emergency management website or call 2-1-1.

Where: Shelters are open inland. Locations are posted on the county's official channels and in the Harborline 6 app. Confirm a location before you drive there.

Rides: County buses are picking up residents who do not have cars. If you already registered through 2-1-1, stay ready. If you did not, call now.

"We are working through the list as fast as we can," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you're waiting on a bus, stay where we can find you. Keep your phone on and charged."

What to bring:

Medicines and a list of doses.

IDs, insurance cards and important papers in a waterproof bag.

Phone chargers and a power bank.

Clothes for several days.

Food for babies or anyone on a special diet.

Pets: bring food, a leash or carrier and vaccination records, and ask about pet arrangements when you call.
