Before you go: unplug appliances, bring in outdoor items, lock up and tell someone where you are headed.

Not in a surge zone? County officials ask you to stay off the roads unless you need to travel so evacuees can get through.

Check on neighbors before you leave, especially older residents and anyone without a car. If they need a ride, help them call 2-1-1.

Harborline 6 is live with updates all day on air, online and in our app.

item.title: Plywood, gas lines and planes overhead: Corpus Christi gets ready for Rafael
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Hardware stores are busy and training aircraft are heading north as Rafael nears. Here is where things stand Friday evening.
item.content:encoded:
The plywood goes fast. By midday, the parking lot at a Southside hardware store is full. Carts roll out stacked with sheets, sandbags, tarps and water.

At the gas stations, lines spill into the street. People top off tanks and fill red cans. Nobody honks. Everybody checks a phone.

Overhead, training aircraft head north. NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville are flying them to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth. At Corpus Christi Army Depot, work has stopped and the helicopters are locked down in hangars.

Marcus Bell, 67, carries a case of batteries and two jugs of water to the register. He has lived on North Beach for decades. "I've done this more times than these kids have had birthdays," he says, nodding at the teenagers stocking shelves. "Buy the batteries before you need the batteries. That's the whole secret."

No hurricane watch is up yet. The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael covers Corpus Christi.

What you need to know tonight:

Find your evacuation zone on the county emergency management website.

No car? Call 2-1-1 to register for an evacuation ride.

County officials say shelter locations will be announced if an evacuation order is issued. Wait for official word.

Keep your tank at least half full. Get cash. Charge everything.

Secure what the wind can throw: patio furniture, grills, trash cans, potted plants. If you are putting up plywood, do it in daylight and do not climb a ladder alone.

Check on older neighbors and anyone who lives alone. Ask whether they have a plan and a ride.

The trainers keep climbing out over Flour Bluff as the sun goes down. Then the sky goes quiet.

item.title: Rafael's cone covers Corpus Christi: what Nueces County says to do now
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: No watches are up yet, but Corpus Christi is in Rafael's forecast cone. County emergency managers say know your zone and register for a ride if you will need one.
item.content:encoded:
The forecast cone for Hurricane Rafael now covers Corpus Christi. No watches are in effect yet for the Coastal Bend.

What comes next: a hurricane watch would mean hurricane conditions are possible here. A warning would mean they are expected. Use the time before either one.

No evacuation order has been issued in Nueces County as of Thursday morning. County emergency managers say now is the time to plan for one.

"If you'd need a ride out, today is the day to call," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Call 2-1-1, give them your address and tell them who's in the house, including pets and anybody with medical needs. That's how we know where to send a bus."

Pruitt said shelter plans are ready. "If an evacuation order comes, shelters will be inland, and we will announce locations before anyone is asked to go," he said. "Don't show up somewhere because you saw it on a post. Wait for us to tell you."

Many households near the bay do not have cars, and bus service gaps make leaving harder. If that is you, register now.

Your checklist today:

Look up your evacuation zone on the county emergency management website.

Pack a go-bag for each person: medicine, IDs, chargers, clothes, snacks.

Fill prescriptions and gas tanks. Get cash.

Plan for pets: carrier, food, leash, records.

Secure outdoor items.

Where to get updates: Nueces County emergency management, the National Weather Service and Harborline 6. We will post every county announcement in our app as it happens.

item.title: Hurricane Rafael: six things to do before any watch is issued
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Rafael became a hurricane, and forecasters warn it could strengthen quickly. No watches are in effect for the Coastal Bend yet. Use the time.
item.content:encoded:
Rafael is now a hurricane. Forecasters warn it could strengthen rapidly over warm Gulf water. As of Wednesday afternoon, nothing is posted for the Coastal Bend: no watch, no warning. That gives you time. Here is how to use it.

1. Know your zone. Look up your address on your county emergency management website. If you are in a hurricane evacuation zone, decide now where you would go and how you would get there.

2. Register for a ride if you need one. County emergency managers urge residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before any order. Call 2-1-1. If you care for someone with medical needs, register them too.

3. Fill prescriptions. Aim for at least a two-week supply. Make a written list of every medication and dose.

4. Fill the tank and get cash. Lines at gas stations grow fast once a watch is issued, and card readers do not work without power.

5. Secure your yard. Bring in or tie down patio furniture, grills, trash cans and anything else wind can throw. Clear storm drains near your home if it is safe. The ground is already saturated from Tuesday's downpours.

6. Charge everything. Phones, power banks, flashlights and radios. Download the Harborline 6 app and turn on alerts.

What not to do: do not share forecast maps from unknown accounts, and do not wait for a watch to start getting ready. Once a watch is issued, stores and gas stations get crowded fast.

Harborline 6 Weather will have Rafael's latest track tonight and every morning this week.

item.title: In Calallen, a teacher watches the river and the school pickup line
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Tropical moisture ahead of Rafael is soaking the area, and the Nueces River is rising. Leticia Ramos is keeping neighbors and families in the loop.
item.content:encoded:
Rain drums on umbrellas in the school pickup line in Calallen. Leticia Ramos stands under the awning with a clipboard and a whistle, waving cars forward one at a time.

Tropical moisture streaming ahead of Rafael and a stalled front are soaking the Coastal Bend. The Nueces River is rising at Calallen. The ground is saturated.

Ramos, 45, teaches in Calallen and lives near the river. She has started a group text with her neighbors. Twice a day, she checks the river gauge online and sends the reading. "No drama. Just what it says," she says. "People like having one person who checks, instead of twenty people guessing."

What she wants is more than a number. "A number on a website isn't a plan," Ramos says. "I want somebody official to tell us what the river means for us. Is it a little high? Is it a problem? Is it a 'move your car' problem?"

A parent rolls down a window to ask whether school will close. Ramos shakes her head. Classes are on. She points to the district alert sign-up flyer taped to the door.

If you live near the river: check the National Weather Service river gauge page for the Nueces at Calallen. Do not drive through water over the road. Move cars out of low spots. Keep your phone charged.

Rafael itself is still far to the south. Forecasts continue to show a west-northwest track toward Texas. Harborline 6 Weather is tracking it.

The last car pulls away. Ramos checks her phone. The group text has twelve new messages. She starts reading.

item.title: Holiday crowds head home from the islands with one eye on Rafael
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: The causeway is busy, the ferry line long and the storm still far to the south in the Caribbean. Forecasters say keep watching.
item.content:encoded:
It's Labor Day afternoon. Coolers are packed. Sunburns are settling in. Cars stack up at the ferry landing, and traffic inches across the JFK Causeway toward the mainland.

Tropical Storm Rafael is still in the Caribbean, far to the south. Early forecasts show a west-northwest track toward Texas. There is still no watch or warning for the Coastal Bend as of Monday afternoon.

At a gas station on Padre Island, a man in a fishing shirt tops off his tank and scrolls a weather app while the pump runs. Two kids in the back seat argue over a bag of chips. Nobody looks worried. A few people look curious.

Port Aransas businesses had a strong summer, and the holiday weekend brought one last rush to the islands. Now the visitors head home. For people who live here, the question is what comes next.

If you live on the Coastal Bend, this is your week to get ready, while stores are calm:

Fill your gas tank.

Refill prescriptions.

Check your kit for water, food, flashlights and batteries.

Look up your evacuation zone.

No car? Call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help. County emergency managers want that list built before any order, not after.

Heading home from the islands tonight? Be patient on the causeway, and do not drive tired. Pull over if you need a break, and keep the radio on for weather updates.

Staying on the islands this week? Know your route back to the mainland, and keep an eye on the forecast. Conditions in the Gulf can change faster than holiday traffic clears.

Harborline 6 Weather will have the latest on Rafael's track tonight at 10 and first thing tomorrow morning.

item.title: Rafael forms: what it means for your Labor Day weekend
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Tropical Storm Rafael is in the Caribbean, and early forecasts point toward Texas. No watches or warnings are in effect for the Coastal Bend. Here is what to do this weekend.
item.content:encoded:
Tropical Storm Rafael formed in the northwestern Caribbean on Saturday. Early forecasts show it crossing the Yucatan into the Gulf, with Texas a possible target.

What we know: Rafael is a tropical storm. Its early track points toward the Texas coast. It is too early to say where it will make landfall or how strong it will be. As of Saturday afternoon, the Coastal Bend is not under any watch or warning.

Your holiday weekend: Port Aransas businesses had a strong summer, and the beaches are busy for Labor Day. Plans can go ahead for now. Check the forecast morning and evening, keep your phone charged and know how you would get off the island if you needed to.

Do these things now, while it is easy:

Fill up the gas tank, and keep it at least half full from here on.

Refill prescriptions you will need over the next two weeks.

Get some cash. Card readers do not work without power.

Check your kit: water, food, flashlights, batteries, chargers.

Look up your evacuation zone on your county emergency management website.

No car? Call 2-1-1 to register for evacuation help. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to sign up before a storm, not during one.

A word about what you see online: forecast maps shared on social media sometimes show a single computer model run, which can swing wildly from one update to the next. Rely on the National Weather Service and your county emergency managers.

Harborline 6 Weather will update Rafael's forecast through the weekend on air, online and in our app.

item.title: Labor Day getaway: expect heavy traffic to the islands and long lines at the ferry
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Holiday crowds are heading for Mustang and Padre islands. Here is how to make the trip easier and safer.
item.content:encoded:
It's Friday afternoon. The holiday weekend is on. Traffic is building on the JFK Causeway toward Padre Island and on the roads to Port Aransas.

Port Aransas businesses have reported a strong summer, and the last long weekend of the season usually brings one more rush. Bait shops and charters are busy. Beaches will be crowded.

Taking the ferry? Waits at the Port Aransas ferry landing in Aransas Pass can run long on holiday weekends. If you are coming from Corpus Christi, consider driving over the JFK Causeway and up Mustang Island on State Highway 361 instead.

Driving on the beach? Keep it slow. Watch for kids, dogs and people walking from their cars to the water. Park above the high-tide line.

Heat is still a factor. Carry more water than you think you need. Take breaks in the shade. Never leave a child or pet in a parked car. The city is still asking residents to conserve water at home.

In the water: swim near a lifeguard stand, check the flags and keep an eye on kids at all times. If you get caught in a current, swim parallel to shore until you are out of it.

Check the forecast before you go. Forecasters expect a busy rest of the hurricane season, and conditions in the Gulf can change over a long weekend. Harborline 6 Weather will update the forecast every morning through Monday.

Heading home Monday? Leave early or late. Midafternoon is when the causeway and the ferry line are usually at their worst.

item.title: North Beach packs in the late-summer crowds as one longtime resident keeps watch from his porch
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Heat, crowds and a reminder to conserve water as summer winds down on North Beach.
item.content:encoded:
North Beach is packed. Saturday afternoon. Umbrellas in rows. Kids in the shallow surf. Cars circling for parking in the shadow of the old aircraft carrier.

Marcus Bell watches it all from a lawn chair on his porch a few blocks from the water. He is 67, a retired welder, and he has lived on North Beach long enough to stop counting summers. "Summer people come and go," Bell says. "The wind stays."

Heavy tourism has filled the beaches on the barrier islands and along the bay all summer. With the heat hanging on, the city keeps urging residents to conserve water. Bell nods toward a neighbor's lawn sprinkler ticking away at three in the afternoon. "City says save water," he says. "That fella hasn't heard."

He notices things. The way the tide sits higher on some evenings. The way the wind swings around before a front. The way the gulls go quiet. "You live on a strip of sand between two bays and a ship channel, you learn to look," he says.

Forecasters expect a busy rest of the hurricane season. Bell keeps his plan short. "I've got water. I've got a radio. I've got a ladder," he says. Asked what the ladder is for, he just raises an eyebrow.

If you are heading to the beach this weekend: bring water, take breaks in the shade and watch for flags on the lifeguard stands. At home, the city asks residents to water lawns early in the morning or late in the evening and to fix leaky faucets and sprinklers.

The crowds will thin after Labor Day. Bell says he will still be on the porch.

item.title: Busy season ahead: Build your hurricane kit before the shelves empty
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Forecasters expect above-normal activity for the rest of the Atlantic season. Here is a kit list and the sign-ups to do this week.
item.content:encoded:
Forecasters are calling for an above-normal rest of the Atlantic hurricane season. That does not mean a storm is coming here. It does mean now is the time to get ready, while the stores are calm and the shelves are full.

Water and food. Plan on at least one gallon of water per person per day for several days, plus food that does not need cooking. Do not forget a manual can opener.

Medicine and documents. Get a refill on prescriptions if you can. Put copies of IDs, insurance policies and medical records in a waterproof bag, and take photos of them on your phone.

Power. Flashlights, batteries, phone chargers and a battery or crank radio. If you use a generator, never run it indoors or in a garage.

Pets. Food, water, a leash or carrier, and vaccination records. Many shelters ask about pets, so plan ahead.

Know your zone. Look up whether your address is in a hurricane evacuation zone on your county emergency management website. If you are in one, decide now where you would go.

Sign up if you will need help. County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation assistance before a storm. Call 2-1-1 to join the state registry. It takes a few minutes.

Check your coverage. Flood damage is usually not covered by homeowners insurance, and new flood policies generally have a waiting period before they take effect.

Harborline 6 Weather will track every system in the Gulf this season. Download our app and turn on alerts, and always check the National Weather Service before sharing a forecast you saw on social media.

item.title: Flour Bluff stargazer knows the night sky over the air station by heart
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Jaime Ortega films the stars from his backyard, and he has learned to tell a satellite from a training plane at a glance.
item.content:encoded:
It's 9 p.m. in Flour Bluff. The heat hangs on. Jaime Ortega sets up a tripod in his backyard and points a camera at the southeast sky.

Ortega, 42, is a hobby astronomer. He films the night sky on most clear evenings and posts the clips online. Planets. Meteors. The International Space Station sliding across without a sound.

He also films a lot of airplanes. Flour Bluff sits next to Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, where training squadrons are flying a normal summer schedule. "You learn the patterns," Ortega says. "Blinking red and green, steady path, engine noise a few seconds behind. That's a plane. That's somebody's student pilot. I don't even look up anymore."

A satellite is different, he explains. No blinking. No sound. A steady glide that fades out as it slips into Earth's shadow.

He keeps a notebook next to the tripod. Time, direction, what he thinks each light was. When he isn't sure, he writes "unknown" and leaves it there. "The sky is full of things people get excited about," he says. "Most of them are airplanes. I'd rather say 'I don't know' than say something that isn't true."

His favorite nights come after a front pushes through and the air clears over the Laguna Madre. This summer, he says, has given him plenty.

Neighbors have started wandering over when they see the tripod. Kids ask about Saturn. Retirees ask about the base. Ortega answers both the same way: look up, be patient, and don't make anything bigger than it is.

"It's free," he says, adjusting the focus. "And it's the only quiet place in town."

item.title: Back to school: How to make sure a storm closure notice reaches you
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Districts across Nueces County are reviewing storm closure plans as classes begin. Here is what parents should check this week.
item.content:encoded:
Classes start across Nueces County this week, and districts are reviewing their storm closure plans before the busiest stretch of hurricane season. Harborline 6 put together a checklist so a closure notice does not slip past you.

Update your contact information. Schools send closure alerts to the phone numbers and email addresses on file. If you changed numbers over the summer, tell the front office this week, not when a storm is on the map.

Opt in to text alerts. Many districts send closure messages by text as well as by phone and email. Check your district's website for how to sign up, and save the district's number in your contacts so messages are not filtered as spam.

Know your pickup plan. If schools close early ahead of a storm, decide now who will pick up your children, and make sure that person is on the school's approved pickup list.

Plan for a ride. County emergency managers have urged residents without cars to register in advance for evacuation assistance. In Texas, that is the State of Texas Emergency Assistance Registry, or STEAR. Sign up by calling 2-1-1. Registering does not commit you to anything, but it helps planners know who will need help.

Keep medicines in mind. If your child takes daily medication, ask the school nurse how it would be handled if campuses close on short notice, and keep a backup supply at home.

Follow one trusted source. Closure decisions come from the districts themselves. Harborline 6 will carry them on air, online and in our app, but check the district's own channels before acting on a forwarded post.

item.title: Peak hurricane season is coming. Here's what to stock now
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Relief agencies are filling their warehouses. Your household can do the same, a little at a time.
item.content:encoded:
Relief agencies across the Coastal Bend are stocking warehouses ahead of the peak of hurricane season. Harborline 6 asked county emergency managers what families should have at home. The answer: more than you think, and sooner than you think.

"Buy a little every time you go to the store," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If you wait for a forecast, so does everybody else, and the shelves are empty."

Your stock list: Water for every person and pet for several days. Nonperishable food that does not need cooking. A manual can opener. Prescription medicines and copies of prescriptions. Flashlights and extra batteries. A battery or hand-crank radio. Phone chargers and a power bank. Cash in small bills. A first-aid kit. Baby and pet supplies if you need them.

Paper matters: Keep IDs, insurance policies, leases and medical information in a waterproof bag. Take photos of them, and of your home's contents, on your phone.

Plan your exit: Know your evacuation zone. If you do not have a car, register for evacuation assistance by dialing 2-1-1. Pick an out-of-town contact for your family and make sure everyone has the number.

Help your neighbors: If you have room in your car, tell a neighbor who does not. Check on older residents and anyone who lives alone.

Do it in pieces: Add one or two items to every grocery run instead of buying everything at once. By the time the season peaks, your kit is done.

item.title: Port Aransas rides a strong summer: charters booked, bait shops busy
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Businesses on Mustang Island say this has been a good season. Here is what to know if you are headed to Port Aransas this weekend.
item.content:encoded:
Port Aransas is having a good summer. Charter boats are booked, the bait shops are busy and restaurants on the island have lines out the door on weekend nights.

Businesses on Mustang Island report a strong season, helped by steady crowds since early summer. At Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties, owner Bill Hargrove says the shop has hardly had a quiet morning.

"I've had people waiting in the parking lot before I unlock the door," Hargrove says. "I asked one fella if he'd been there all night. He said, 'Not all night.'"

Anglers have been working the jetties, the surf and the bays, and kids are catching their first fish off the piers. Charter captains are running full trips on most weekends.

Headed over this weekend? Expect waits for the ferry at midday. Arriving early, or coming in from the south on the JFK Causeway and Highway 361, can help. Park only where it is allowed and check local beach rules before you drive on the sand.

Bring some cash for the smaller shops and bait stands, and be patient at the fuel docks and boat ramps, which are busiest early in the morning and again in the late afternoon.

Around the jetties, keep a close eye on kids. The rocks are slick and sharp, and big ships passing through the channel can push wakes onto the rocks without much warning.

Heat safety still applies. Take breaks in the shade, drink water and watch for signs of heat illness, including dizziness, headache and confusion.

Harborline 6 will be on the island this weekend. Send us your best catch photo.

item.title: Two ways off North Beach: summer crowds test the Harbor Bridge and the causeway
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Heavy summer traffic is backing up the routes in and out of North Beach on weekends. Residents say the bridges are their lifeline.
item.content:encoded:
Summer weekends on North Beach end the same way: a slow crawl toward the Harbor Bridge. Visitors leave the sand, the aquarium and the museum ship at about the same time, and the line of cars stretches back along the beach road.

North Beach sits on a narrow strip of land between Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay. There are two ways off by car: the Harbor Bridge south to downtown, and the Nueces Bay Causeway north toward Portland. When one backs up, the other fills.

Marcus Bell, 67, has lived on North Beach long enough to plan his errands around it. "Saturday and Sunday, I don't go anywhere after lunch," says Bell, a retired welder. "You go over that bridge at 4 o'clock, you'd better have a full tank and a good radio station."

Tips for summer weekends: Head home before late afternoon if you can. Check traffic before you leave the beach. Keep water in the car, because idling in the sun gets hot fast. Watch your gas gauge, since both routes include long stretches of bridge with nowhere to pull off.

If you break down on a bridge, stay in your vehicle with your seat belt on, turn on your hazard lights and call 911.

Bell says the beach traffic is the price of living somewhere people want to visit. "I'll take it. It's pretty out here," he says. "But you learn real quick, out here the bridge isn't just a road. It's the door."

Harborline 6 posts weekend traffic updates for the Harbor Bridge, the Nueces Bay Causeway and the JFK Causeway on our Traffic page.

item.title: Advocates push for more evacuation rides for families without cars
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Neighborhood leaders near the bay say a registry is not enough. Here is how to sign up for evacuation help now.
item.content:encoded:
In neighborhoods near the bay, a lot of families do not have a car. Advocates say that has to change how Corpus Christi plans for a storm.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield runs a relief hub out of her church's fellowship hall. She says bus gaps already leave many of her neighbors stuck at night and on weekends, and an evacuation would be harder still. "Registering is step one," Whitfield tells Harborline 6. "Step two is somebody actually showing up. I want to see more rides, more pickup spots and people knocking on doors."

Nueces County emergency managers are urging residents without cars to register for evacuation help now, before any storm. "If you don't have a way out, tell us now," says Dwayne Pruitt, the public information officer for the county's emergency management office. "That's how we know where to send help."

How to register: Dial 2-1-1 and ask for the state's emergency assistance registry. You can register yourself or help a neighbor do it. It is not only for people with disabilities. If you will not have a ride, it is for you.

Make a backup plan: Ask a neighbor, relative or church member with a car whether they can take you. Write their number down on paper, not just in your phone. Keep a bag packed with medicines, documents and phone chargers.

Know your zone: Look up your evacuation zone on the county's website, or ask at one of the county's preparedness fairs this summer.

Harborline 6 will keep following the push for more evacuation rides.

item.title: Fact check: Evacuation help is not just for people with disabilities. No car? Sign up.
item.dc:creator: Keisha Monroe
item.description: Some residents believe the state's evacuation assistance registry is only for people with medical needs. County emergency managers say anyone who would need a ride should register.
item.content:encoded:
The claim: Harborline 6 viewers have told us they skipped signing up for evacuation help because they heard the registry is "only for people in wheelchairs" or "only for people on oxygen."

The verdict: False. Nueces County emergency managers are urging residents who do not have a car to register for evacuation assistance, whether or not they have a disability or a medical need.

"If you don't have a way to leave, you're who this is for," says Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "Don't talk yourself out of it. Let us figure out what help you need."

The county has been making that pitch at hurricane-season preparedness fairs this summer. At one Wednesday, as the Bayside Ledger reported, staff handed registration cards to families who get around by bus.

How to sign up: Dial 2-1-1 and ask to join the state's emergency assistance registry. You will be asked for your address, how many people live with you and what kind of help you would need. A relative, neighbor or church volunteer can help you register.

What it is not: Registering does not guarantee a ride at a specific time, so it should not replace your own plan. Know your evacuation zone, keep a go-bag ready and line up a neighbor or relative who can drive you if possible.

Why it matters: Emergency planners use the registry to understand who in their community may need help and what kind. If people who need a ride are not on it, planners cannot count them.

Bottom line: If you will not have a car when an evacuation order comes, sign up now.

item.title: Islands are packed this weekend: what to know before you head to the beach
item.dc:creator: Tyler Brandt
item.description: Heavy summer crowds are filling Mustang and Padre islands. Here is how to beat the lines and the heat.
item.content:encoded:
The islands are full. Cars line up for the Port Aransas ferry before breakfast, and beach parking on Mustang and North Padre islands is filling fast this Saturday as summer crowds pour onto the coast.

If you are heading out, plan for heat and plan for waiting. Bring more water than you think you need. Pack shade. Check the ferry status before you leave, or take the JFK Causeway onto Padre Island and drive north on Highway 361 to reach Mustang Island from the south.

At Hargrove Bait & Tackle near the jetties in Port Aransas, owner Bill Hargrove has been opening early. "Busiest I've seen it in a while. Everybody wants shrimp, ice and directions, in that order," Hargrove says. "I only charge for two of those."

City water officials are also asking residents to go easy on the tap while the heat holds. Water lawns early or late, and only on your scheduled day.

Heat safety: Watch for dizziness, headache, nausea and confusion. Move anyone showing those signs into shade, cool them with water and call 911 if symptoms get worse or the person stops sweating.

Rip currents: Swim near lifeguards where they are on duty, and obey the beach flags. If a current pulls you out, do not fight it. Swim parallel to the shore until you are free, then swim back in.

Leave the dunes alone: Park only in marked or allowed areas, and keep vehicles off the dunes and out of soft sand you are not sure about.

Harborline 6 will update beach and traffic conditions through the weekend.
